A second is a moment. To children! A second is a measure of life! What does a second measure? A second is an earthly, real measure with which we, at any moment we wish, can measure any episode of our life—its length, its beginning and end, and even its place on the “event tape” of that day, on the “tape of existence”! The place that I record every second (every second!), at any moment of the day, on the dial of a clock—a mechanism that, just as reliably and accurately, always measures every step on this part of the Earth, every moment of our lives, and also measures the static (standard) length of this rotation of the Earth (a day!), all its 86,400 parts (moments of existence), and arranges them not in a stack, not in a bag, not even in a file, but in a circular row on the clock’s dial—as a record of all the minutes and hours of the day—measures! And the big hand of the clock (at this moment!) points to the place in the day (the point, the moment of this day) where I (and the whole world!) am, where I am living now!. A second is an empty, old word, a mistaken concept, because in the dark ages it measured not BEING, not life, but the “time” invented by the pharaohs and philosophers of Babylon — which, of course, was not real, visible, obvious, or understandable! If the measures “gram” or “meter” are real, obvious, understandable, and consistent in weight or length, then “second” has never even seen WHAT it measures, is not even familiar with the word “time,” and is not friends with anyone; it exists indifferently, uninterestingly, boringly—after all, it is a measure shaped, measured, and created by human hands?! An unnoticed, indispensable worker. A second – it doesn’t rush, doesn’t hurry, doesn’t push, doesn’t drag on, doesn’t stretch, doesn’t accelerate; it’s not relative (doesn’t relate) to anything (just like a centimeter or a 1‑kilogram weight), it doesn’t fly, doesn’t have a direction or speed… just like the measures “minute,” “hour,” “day,” “year”! There is: her short, small length, which imperceptibly, non‑stop, and coolly measures, records, sets aside, and files every moment of life into the “minute” file. It doesn’t care whether a turtle is crawling or a bison is fleeing in fear. But it always informs every person, provides invaluable information: “You are not making it by the end of the day, by the deadline; you are running late!” A second measures existence, my sleep, all the events of the universe! Here is the Truth: “A second is the measure of life!” It doesn’t get along with, isn’t even familiar with the empty word “time.” It is Man himself who assigns and uses it — the same measure to measure different (all) moments of life! Unlike the word “time” (an ancient fake created by power and religion), a second is material, real (and not just the mechanism of the alarm clock itself!), obvious, understandable; it can be filled with a clap, the sound of music, a voice, and even the Beat of the Heart (the prototype of a second), the pulse of a living person! A second is a measure of life (of all episodes of life!) and a measure of this day! A measure of measuring a part, a segment of eternal existence. A second is a real, noticeable, obvious, eternal, static measure created by us to measure life: the life of a person, a planet, a country, a frog, a dolphin! A second is a measure of all events, activities, their duration, their beginning and end, their place in the queue, in the chaos, surrounded by other events on the “event timeline of this day”! This is how we get (have) a clear order of things and notice, mark (take into account!) The causes and effects of all phenomena and events, their “cause-and-effect” relationships! Only the quick-witted, hasty astrophysicists of the planet lack logic in their fabrication about the nature of the “singular point” of the Big Bang; they have neither a cause nor an explanation or understanding of the central falsification of their Theory of Everything!? Seconds add up, filling the measures: minute, hour, day (twenty‑four hours), and days (a day is the Earth’s rotation) fill the “files of life measurement”: week, month, year! It is because of the mistakes made by these scientists that we, you and I, end up with the “MAIN QUESTION OF COSMOLOGY” from Wikipedia, and its main error: “How did the Universe come into being?”!??.. But this idea is precisely the cause of all the troubles on the planet, the reason for the emergence of millions of fake dissertations, publications, and theories from organized, powerful groups. After all, it is obvious and likely that the emptiness of space is ETERNAL, just like its adornment; the meaning and purpose of its existence a MAN — or, more precisely, humanity as a whole!

“Scientists can track that developing pattern from space because warming water expands, raising the sea surface.”

The sea surface is moved by tides, drifting air masses with different pressures, prevailing winds, random gusts, constructive interference of waves from all over the world, and ubiquitous, local waves. Those influences, many with short temporal duration, have to be averaged to obtain an estimate of the mean surface elevation. I have never seen an estimate of the standard deviation, often used as an estimate for the uncertainty of the mean. Things like “rogue waves,” (constructive/destructive interference) are probably usually missed, despite their great height, because of their short duration and narrow width.

Why the preference for altimetry instead of a direct measure of temperature? Because of surface mixing and the thermal inertia of water, it would seem to me that thermal IR would be a more direct measurement of the influence of El Niño on weather.

Once again, it appears necessary to remind these authors, and others, that “could” is a qualitative, not quantitative, word used to describe a low-probability event that is not, however, impossible. That is, it is permissive, not obligatory. In fact, the way it is commonly used, it has less probability of occurring than not occurring. Given that it is not associated with a numeric probability, there isn’t much else about it that can be said that is actionable. It is a word best used by a defense attorney trying to convince a jury that it is possible that his/her client is innocent of the charges brought. Our jurisprudence system is purposely designed to minimize wrongful convictions. It is embodied in the guiding principle that it is better that 10 guilty criminals are set free rather than one innocent person be punished. Science is not supposed to have such biases.

If this developing El Niño turns out to not be as strong or long-lasting as it ‘could’ be, will we hear any more about it after the fact? Will we get an explanation for why it didn’t live up to the arm waving? Probably not, because meteorologists don’t really know what triggers an El Niño. About the best they can do is predict that they will occur episodically every two to seven years. They are like a great earthquake or volcanic eruption in that respect.

#6494. Tiny Solar Whirlpools May Hold the Secret to the Sun’s Blistering Corona

For the second time in a few weeks, weâre writing about research into the temperature gap between the Sunâs surface and its corona. More and more data from various missions continue to feed this wave of discovery. A new paper by Katariina Nykyri of Embry-Riddle, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds to this growing body of work. She argues that millions of tiny whirlpools scattered across the Sunâs surface could be the energetic engine driving that temperature difference.

Earlier this year, the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST), located atop HaleakalÄ on Maui, took extremely high resolution images of the Sunâs surface. For the first time, scientists could make out whirlpools of plasma, a few dozen kilometers across, dotted around the Sunâs surface. When this research was published in August, Dr. Nykyri had a bit of a âEureka!â moment, according to a press release from the University.

Her research had focused on Kelvin-Helmholtz waves. On Earth, these are most commonly seen in broken ocean swells or ripple-pattern clouds. However, they are also present elsewhere in the solar system, driving gas patterns on Jupiter. On the Sun, they occur when fast-moving plasma passes slower, magnetized plasma. They contain an absurd amount of mechanical energy. The vortices created by these waves are the very structures DKIST resolved on our starâs surface. As these vortices churn across the solar surface, their vast kinetic energy transfers into the Sun's magnetic fields, converting mechanical motion into magnetic stress.

Fraser talks about the features of the Sun that we are only now getting a glimpse of thanks to new technologies.

Dr. Nykyri set out to answer how much energy these vortices carry and whether it equals the total energy needed to heat the corona. After accounting for the velocity shear, density difference, and vertical heights of the tornadoes, she reached a conclusion. On average, each vortex contains around two septillion ergsâa unit of energy commonly used in solar physics. Across the Sunâs 1.4-million-kilometer surface, millions of these vortices spin up and dissipate every few minutes.

When these vortices dissipate, their energy must go somewhere. According to Dr. Nykyri, it appears to enter the corona through magnetic reconnection. Solar physicists have long thought this process plays a key role in coronal heating. As each KH vortex spins, it squeezes nearby magnetic field lines together. This forms ultra-thin current lines ranging from a few centimeters to meters across.

Once theyâre squeezed past a certain point, they start to violently snap and rearrange. That is the process of magnetic reconnection, and it converts the stored magnetic energy into heat and high-speed plasma jets that are fundamental components of the solar corona. In other words, the KH vortices are the driving force behind the process of reconnection of the Sunâs magnetic field lines.

Frase talks about how hot the Sun actually is.

When the energy they store is released, it has to have somewhere to go, though. And these vortices donât always cause reconnections only in the corona - they also do so on the surface. So why does the corona seem so much hotter? Particle density.

When a magnetic line snaps on the surface, the energy is immediately distributed between trillions of neutral atoms. Each atomâs temperature is commensurately raised, but only by a tiny amount. In the corona, though, atoms are much less plentiful, but the same amount of energy is released. So each magnetic snap increases the temperature of an individual atom by much more in the corona than down on the surface.

According to the paper, only five to eight percent of the mechanical energy stored in the vortices needs to make the journey upward to the corona to replenish the heat that is otherwise radiated away. Even in darker âcoronal holesâ, a max of 21% of the energy from the vortices would be capable of maintaining the temperature of the corona.

This work is a major step toward understanding the heating process, but more research is needed. Scientists still must track wave transmission and polarization through the chromosphere. This will confirm whether as much energy reaches the Sunâs chromosphere as Dr. Nykyri suggests is necessary to maintain coronal temperatures. If her theory holds, some of the high temperatures on our star will be proven to stem from relatively small plasma tornadoes floating across its surface.

The Vikings are famous for being warriors, but how often did Viking women take part in battles?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vikings were explorers, farmers, merchants and, most famously, warriors who launched raids across large parts of Europe.

Stereotypes of Vikings usually conjure up images of muscular men. But over the past few decades, researchers have turned their attention to women of the Viking Age (roughly A.D. 793 to 1066) and the roles they held. For instance, there are stories of "shield maidens" who fought alongside men, and some of these texts mention Viking women who fought in battle. The archaeological record also holds evidence, including graves of Viking Age women who were buried with war-grade weapons and shields.

It's still a matter of debate whether women who lived during the Viking Age could be warriors, but this discussion raises another question: It's one thing to have texts describing female fighters and archaeological records of women buried with weapons, but what can the evidence tell us about how frequently Viking women fought in battle?

The answer, experts told Live Science, largely depends on our interpretation of texts, artifacts, and burials of Viking Age women, which often face higher scrutiny than burials of men who were buried with similar (or even fewer) weapons.

The Vikings used a runic system of writing, but they left precious few texts behind. Instead, much of what we know about the Vikings was written about them by people from other cultures or by their Norse descendants.

One of the most evocative texts was written in the 12th century by the Danish historian and theologian Saxo Grammaticus. In "Gesta Danorum" (Latin for "History of the Danes" and translated by Jenny Jochens), he wrote that "there were once women in Denmark who dressed themselves to look like men and spent almost every minute cultivating [combat] skills." As "if they were forgetful of their true selves they put toughness before allure, aimed at conflicts instead of kisses, tasted blood, not lips, sought the clash of arms rather than the arm's embrace, fitted to weapons hands what should have been weaving, desired not the couch but the kill, and those they could have appeased with looks they attacked with lances."

Another text about the Vikings, the medieval Irish "Cogadh Gaedhelre Gallaibh" ("War of the Irish with the Foreigners"), refers to a woman known as the "Red Lady" leading a Viking fleet in a raid on Belfast in the 10th century.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

There's a lot of uncertainty, said Neil Price, an archaeology professor at Uppsala University in Sweden who has written extensively about the Vikings. The text in the "Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh" that refers to the Red Lady is of debatable accuracy, Price told Live Science in an email.

He suspects that Viking women fought in battle but not frequently. In addition, "female warriors were probably a very small minority," Price said.

A modern-day reenactment depicting Viking warriors.

The account written by Saxo Grammaticus is also contentious. Thomas Kristian Heebøll-Holm, a history professor at the University of Southern Denmark, said Saxo Grammaticus is not a reliable source.

"Saxo Grammaticus does write about female warriors, but only in the parts of his work concerned [with] the legendary past of Denmark," Heebøll-Holm told Live Science in an email. "Furthermore, these writings are not accurate, but moral and fictitious," Heebøll-Holm said, noting that, in some instances, Saxo Grammaticus seemed to be drawing on the stories of the Amazons, a group of legendary female warriors whom the ancient Greeks believed in with stories about them dating back more than 2,500 years.

Archaeological evidence can also be challenging to interpret. Archaeologists know of about 30 Viking Age female burials containing weapons, including three with swords in Scandinavia. Even more Viking Age women's graves have items that could have been used as weapons ‪—‬ including spears, axes and knives ‪—‬ although these tools also could have been used for hunting or tending to farms. Either way, we can't be sure if these women fought in battle.

"The first concern is that the weapons were really used by the deceased and were not merely included as signs of special status or social rank acquired through inheritance," Deborah Shepherd, an independent researcher who holds a doctorate in archaeology and has studied the Vikings extensively, told Live Science in an email. She noted that graves are often not well preserved, making it difficult to gather information.

This 1889 illustration shows a grave at Birka in Sweden. It is now known that the person buried with war-grade weapons and riding gear is a woman.

There were likely "some few female warriors, but they were probably only found in the highest ranking families, and their warrior career was probably short-lived," Shepherd said. "They wouldn't have fought in the great armies of later centuries but possibly did fight in pre-Christian skirmishes." (The Vikings began gradually converting to Christianity between the ninth and 12th centuries.)

There is at least one known case of a Viking woman found with what may be combat-related injuries. A Viking woman found in Solør, Norway, had a head injury consistent with a sword strike. She was 18 or 19 at the time she died, was buried with weapons and lived around 900.

Ole Kastholm, a curator and senior researcher at the Roskilde Museum in Denmark, said there is a lot of uncertainty regarding how frequently Viking Age women fought in battle.

Weapons "do occur as a grave good in a handful of graves with female human remains," Kastholm told Live Science in an email. "Often it is just a single weapon [such] as a spear or [a] battle axe. But we know of at least one example of a female grave with a full set of weapons as well as riding equipment," which is located in Birka, Sweden.

"If this was a man's grave, researchers would have no doubt that it was a warrior grave, and this explanation must necessarily also apply when the interred is a woman," Kastholm said.

That said, there were female warriors in other cultures. "One can also note in passing that female warriors were an almost common feature of central Asian societies for at least a millennium before the Viking Age," Price wrote in his book, "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026).

For instance the Scythians are a people who flourished in eastern Europe and Asia and Scythian women have been found buried with horses and weapons. In some cases, the Scythian women suffered combat wounds such as arrowheads and it's been speculated that they may have been an inspiration for stories of the Amazons.

He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6491. Why Aging Stars Suffer A Sudden Luminosity Dip

From a naked eye perspective, stars are stable and predictable. Not much goes on but shining. The Sun itself is fairly plane and nondescript and will shine relatively steadily for billions of years. It's considered a low-mass star compared to the most massive stars, which are rarer and contain many times its mass.

Powerful telescopes bring millions of stars of different types and ages into view. Astrophysicists and astronomers watch the Sun and its low-mass brethren, and note changes in their shining, just as they do all types of stars. Their observations reveal the changes stars experience during their long lifetimes.

As low-mass stars like the Sun exhaust their hydrogen supplies and evolve, they become Red Giant Branch (RGB) stars. This is not only theoretical, it's an observational conclusion. RGB stars are easy to observe and study for two reasons: they're bright, and they're numerous. Arcturus, Aldebaran, and Pollus are all bright, naked-eye stars and are all RGB stars. (Well-known Betelgeuse is a Red Supergiant, not quite the same.)

As RGB stars age and cool, they swell in size and become more luminous. It's a pretty steady change. But for some reason, there's a brief and abrupt dip in their brightness known as the RGB luminosity bump. The bump is called that because of how it appears in the colourâmagnitude diagrams of stellar clusters.

Astrophysicists know why the bump ends. But what initiates the bump is still unexplained. Astrophysicists don't like this gap in their knowledge and they've been trying to fill it in.

New research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters has an explanation for the bump. It's titled "The Role of Specific Entropy in the Onset of the Luminosity Bump," and the sole author is Saskia Hekker. Hekker is a Professor of Theoretical Astrophysics and the Group Leader of the Theory and Observations of Stars Group at the Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies.

"During their evolution, stars follow a distinct path in luminosityâtemperature space. Low-mass stars that have exhausted hydrogen in their core follow the so-called red-giant branch (RGB), which is predominantly in the direction of increasing luminosity and decreasing surface temperature," Hekker explains. "The luminosity bump is a temporary decrease in luminosity against this otherwise increasing trend."

The inset grey box is the Hertzsprung-Russel diagram for a 1 solar mass star progressing from the subgiant branch to the tip of the Red Giant Branch. The tiny grey box inside it is magnified in the larger part of the image, highlighting the RGB luminosity bump. Image Credit: S. Hekker 2026 ApJL 1008 L61

The bump is understood theoretically and also confirmed with observations. But there's one discrepancy between theory and observation. In models, the bump appears at higher luminosities than the observed bump, meaning it appears later. "To understand why the bump appears later in the models than in observations, the physics of the bump needs to be unravelled," Hekker writes.

Stars, including our Sun, are layered, and RGB stars are no exception. But unlike the Sun, RGB stars have exhausted the hydrogen in their cores, and most of what's left is in their envelopes. Since the core has exhausted its hydrogen by fusing it into helium, the core is inert helium. An RGB's fusion occurs in a thin shell. In both these regions, energy is transported via radiation.

Above this radiative region is a convective outer envelope.

As an RGB star ascends the branch, the core contracts and the surface expands. Since the core is inert helium, it exerts no outward pressure and is forced inward. "This causes the deepest layer of the convective envelope to move inwards, reaching layers that have changed their chemical composition due to (burning) processes earlier in the evolution of the star," Hekker explains.

This is when dredge-up occurs, as deeper layers are forced into the convective zone. Since the convective zone is convective, the material from the radiative zone mixes into the convective zone, changing its composition.

Now there's a situation where there's a shifting boundary deep inside the star called the Base of the Convective Zone (BCZ). It's organized around a thermodynamic property called specific entropy. It basically measures how disordered the gas is at the BCZ. As the BCZ moves deeper inside the star, the entropy difference across the boundary shrinks. Past a certain point, entropy across the boundary layer drops past a critical value, and that triggers the luminosity bump.

This diagram shows the interior of an RGB star (not to scale). An inert helium core is in the center, and it's contained in a thin hydrogen-burning shell. Above that is a radiative zone separated from the star's convective envelope by the base of the convective zone (BCZ). Earlier dredge-up and mixing created this boundary between helium-enriched and hydrogen-rich gas. This work ties the RGB luminosity bump to this boundary. The author argues that the onset of the bump occurs when the entropy across this boundary crosses a critical value. (Image Generated with AI)

Previous explanations for the bump rested on mechanics. In those explanations, the thin hydrogen-burning shell reaches the boundary and something inside the star changes, triggering the bump. In this explanation, the bump happens when an entropy threshold is crossed inside the star's thermodynamics. It's not simply that layers meet.

We can't see inside stars. Astrophysicists use physics to try to understand what's going on there, and they test those physics against the only part of the star they can really see, the outside. It's a constant back and forth to refine theories until they match observations.

âThis succinct explanation of the onset of the bump, is the first quantitative description proposed so far,â said Hekker.

This new work will make its way into the larger body of astrophysical theory.

"This viable description of the mechanism behind the onset of the bump provides crucial and new insights for the exploitation of the bump as an anchor point in stellar evolution theory," Hekker writes. "Such added knowledge of the onset of the bump could potentially be used to make more informed choices for changes to the physics in stellar models that go beyond calibration of the overshoot, to place the bump in stellar evolution models at the correct luminosity while at the same time aligning them with measured surface abundances."

#6490. Antarctica’s Melting Ice Has Triggered a Sudden Shift Deep in the Ocean

Ocean measurements show a vast Southern Hemisphere water layer growing saltier and denser, a shift that could send more heat into deep waters than climate models predict.

Every Antarctic summer, melting sea ice sends a vast pulse of fresh water into the ocean. That seasonal supply helps sustain Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), a layer of relatively fresh seawater that spreads across much of the Southern Hemisphere’s ocean. The AAIW helps store carbon, supply oxygen, and drive global currents, redistributing heat, fresh water, and carbon around the planet.

From 1995 to 2015, summer ice melt helped maintain this layer. But from 2016 to 2024, reduced freshwater input left it saltier, denser, and deeper, abruptly reversing its long-term trends in salinity, or salt content, and density.

The findings, published in Nature Climate Change, provide the first direct observational evidence of this change in the AAIW’s properties. The international research team analyzed data from the global Argo program, a network of around 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans, alongside satellite and atmospheric datasets.

The study was led by Associate Professor Bishakhdatta Gayen, of the University of Melbourne and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), and Kaushik Mishra, a PhD student at IISc. Gayen said:

“The Antarctic region is the freshwater engine of oceans around the globe. Melting Antarctic sea ice influences circulation thousands of kilometers away. Until 2016, the seasonal summer melt was triple the Amazon River’s entire annual flow of roughly 6,600 cubic km.

“From 2016, Antarctic sea ice shrank to record lows. This abruptly choked off that critical seasonal surge, and the meltwater delivery dropped to roughly double the Amazon’s annual flow.”

Co-author Professor Alberto Naveira Garabato, of the University of Southampton in the United Kingdom, described the changes as an urgent reminder that climate change is affecting almost every part of Earth’s surface.

“As this altered, saltier and denser water mass travels north, it moves across the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Because this water layer forms part of the upper limb of the ocean’s global ‘overturning circulation’, a sustained shift could, over years to decades, feed into the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation – the deep-ocean current system often linked to climate stability in the North Atlantic.

“It could also ultimately influence atmospheric circulation, weather, and storm tracks in the Southern Hemisphere. However, the impact can cascade globally.”

The globe shows sea ice around Antarctica month by month. The first time-series graph shows whether sea-ice area was above or below normal (the 1993-2024 mean), based on satellite observations. The bottom graph tracks the saltiness of Antarctic Intermediate Water, a layer that sinks from the surface into the ocean’s interior, using Argo float data from 2004. From 1993 to 2015, Antarctic sea ice slowly expanded (blue trend line), releasing more freshwater, making the waters beneath it fresher. After 2016, sea ice dropped sharply (red trend line), and the layer turned saltier. Less melting ice means less freshwater reaching the ocean interior. Credit: Kaushik Mishra

Changes in how water moves between the surface and deeper layers could also affect the oceans’ role as a “climate buffer,” as Gayen described it. Oceans absorb and redistribute most of the excess heat and a large share of human CO₂ emissions, storing them for decades to centuries. This slows and moderates atmospheric warming and its immediate effects.

Mishra said the abrupt reversal revealed a critical missing feedback loop.

“The ocean absorbs over 90 percent of all heat released into the environment by human activities, with most of that heat stored in the upper ocean. A weakened AAIW layer could push more excess heat deeper. That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures.”

“If the altered AAIW changes the way surface water is carried down into deeper layers, it could affect how much carbon the ocean locks away – although the magnitude and timing are uncertain,” Gayen said.

“This could be the tipping point for the Atlantic Ocean and the AAIW current, leading to larger, longer-lasting changes to the climate in the Southern Hemisphere.”

According to Gayen, the last time the AAIW switched was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in Antarctica.

“That transition took thousands of years, not two decades,” he said.

Reference: “Reversal of Antarctic Intermediate Water trends triggered by sea ice decline” by Kaushik Mishra, Bishakhdatta Gayen and Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, 28 October 2026, Nature Climate Change. DOI: 10.1038/s41558-026-02758-y

MOES/11/2024) and the Australian Research Council Discovery Grant (grant no. DP240102823). A.C.N.G. acknowledges U.K. Research and Innovation guarantee funding for a European Research Council Advanced Grant (grant no. EP/X025136/1).

“Every Antarctic summer, melting sea ice sends a vast pulse of fresh water into the ocean.”

Inexplicably, the authors don’t mention why the melting sea ice is ‘fresh.’ Obviously, there is some snow on top of the ice. However, the main reason is that as sea water freezes, the dissolved salts are extruded from the crystal lattice of the forming ice, and cold, dense plums of concentrated brine sink into the depths. They have ignored half of the cycle and focused on the melting half, and implied that recent behavior portends a change in the long-term trend. Predictions are difficult when a system isn’t rigorously characterized and understood, which is the case with Antarctica. Antarctic shelf ice is is notoriously variable, and thus highly unpredictable. This is Chicken Little behavior of the wet feathers variety.

“That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures.”

Water is incompressible. Therefore, thermosteric expansion of the deep water by the speculated warming will be communicated to the sea level surface. Where is the evidence that this is happening?

But most of all, I love that this thing is guaranteed to work for life.”

MoMA Design Store Bodum Neon Nesting Mixing Bowls (Set of 4)

As a person who drinks coffee every day (and feels horrified when I run out), I would be thrilled to receive this American Girl doll-sized bag (weighing 4 pounds) of beans from the award-winning Joshua Tree Coffee. This year, the Big Bag — which is filled with the beans of your choice — even comes with a cute enamel mug.

Joshua Tree Coffee Big Bag & Bellied Enamel Mug Bundle

The Chitose is kind of like the Ferrari of kettles, because it boils water extremely fast and is made out of professional-grade, scratch-resistant 18-8 stainless steel. Plus, it cuts a cute silhouette and is compatible with induction top stoves.

Japanese Taste Chitose Induction Compatible Japanese Stainless Steel Kettle

These pastel eggnog petit fours come from the acclaimed Los Angeles-based confectionary Valerie Confections, and are made of a rich spiced buttercake, with bourbon ganache layers dipped in white chocolate and garnished with 23-karat gold leaf and chocolate biscuit pearls.

Ghia’s apéritif box is one of those drink-themed holiday gifts that sells out every year, because it pairs the brand’s signature amaro-esque N/A ambrosia with chic glassware from French-American glass artist and designer Sophie Lou Jacobsen. Whether you’re shopping for someone who doesn’t drink or is just trying to drink less alcohol in the new year, it’s a fashionable foot forward in the world of booze-free drinks.

Owning a double burner griddle is the culinary equivalent to flexing a California king size bed, because it can handle all of the pancakes, eggs, and grilled cheese orders from the family (without having to hop between skillets like a stove DJ). Eater collaborated with heritage crystal glassware company Zwiesel Fortessa on a collection of timeless pieces, including this versatile set of six Nick and Nora-style glasses.

Eater x Zwiesel Fortessa Folly Crystal Glass, 6 Ounce Cocktail (Set of 6)

Sometimes the best present is one that contains even more presents: a giant box of Swedish candies, all curated by the cult-fave confectioners at BonBon. Dubbed the Holiday Connoisseur Box, this light pink coffret is filled with classic BonBon gummies (I spy Pippi Longstocking’s Gold Coins) and plenty of Swedish classics like Marabou Japp chocolate bars and Juleskum marshmallow candies.

Kudos to Emma Chamberlain on this postmodern-feeling French press. The YouTuber went viral yet again for her collaboration with West Elm, and this coffee press in particularly takes notes from its elders (Bodum and Alessi) with its sleek stainless steel design.

Emma Chamberlain x West Elm Stainless Steel Button French Press

John Derian is the Final Boss of curating swish food-themed holiday ornaments (I do also need this energy drink-themed ornament), so it’s hardly surprising that the New York-based designer plucked this boneless cooked ham ornament for this year’s batch of stunners.

#6487. First Direct Measurement of Cosmic Hydrogen Could Change How We Map the Universe

Advances in computing and astronomy have led to increasingly complex attempts to chart the large-scale structure of the Universe. For the past decade, scientists have been working to map one aspect in particular to see whether it matches observations of the cosmic web: cosmic hydrogen. For the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang, neutral hydrogen was the only element in the Universe (known as the "Cosmic Dark Ages") and provided the feedstock for stars, galaxies, and the cosmic web.

Today, it remains the most abundant element in the Universe and can be found everywhere - the interstellar medium (ISM) and the intergalactic medium (IGM) - in abundance. For the past decade, scientists with the MeerKLASS Collaboration have been trying to measure how neutral hydrogen "clumps" in the distant Universe. In a study published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), the team announced the first direct measurement of the large-scale structure of cosmic hydrogen.

The MeerKLASS (MeerKAT Large Area Synoptic Survey) Collaboration is an international group of astronomers conducting cosmological surveys using the MeerKAT radio telescope. Their survey relies on a technique known as HI intensity (or 21-cm intensity) mapping to detect the combined emissions of galaxies within large segments of the sky. This enables the creation of 3D maps of the cosmos that show the distribution of matter (gas, dust, stars, galaxies, clusters, etc.) in the cosmic web.

Members of the MeerKLASS collaboration at their biannual 'Busy Week' meeting, hosted at the University of Torino in September 2025. Credit: SARAO

This is no easy task, since the 21-cm signal must be extracted from all the other emissions of the Universe (the "foreground noise"), which are about 10,000 times stronger than the hydrogen signal itself. To accomplish this, the team chose to operate each dish in the array as an independent telescope, rather than combining all 64 dishes into a single interferometer. This was an entirely new observation mode for MeerKAT that traded sharp angular resolution for very high survey speed.

For their survey, the team analyzed data collected by the MeerKAT array across ~250 square degrees of sky. This enabled the detection of a neutral hydrogen signal that originated 4.5 billion years ago (or 9 billion years after the Big Bang). The team's measurements produced many independent maps from different dishes and observing times. These were then cross-compared to suppress individual instrument effects and reinforce the structure of cosmic hydrogen.

Their results showed that cosmic hydrogen mirrors the large-scale structure of the cosmic web, advancing a technique that could transform how cosmologists map the Universe. Dr Steven Cunnington, a Senior Research Fellow at Purdue University's Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation, led the development of the analysis pipeline that enabled the mapping of cosmic hydrogen. Since 2015, he has also co-led one of the working groups within the MeerKLASS Collaboration.

As he expressed in a University of Portsmouth release:

This result feels particularly special because it's the culmination of a journey that began when I started my PhD at Portsmouth over a decade ago. I am now fortunate to be part of a much wider international collaboration sharing this common goal. Many of the challenges addressed in this work have shaped my own research career, so seeing our team deliver this measurement is a remarkable milestone to witness.

This slice of the DESI data maps celestial objects from Earth (center) to billions of light-years away, showing nearby bright galaxies (yellow), luminous red galaxies (orange), emission-line galaxies (blue), and quasars (green). Credit: DESI Collaboration/DOE/KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/C. Lamman

This information can be used to constrain the most pressing cosmological measurements facing scientists today. This includes the expansion rate of the cosmos (the Hubble-LemaÃ®tre Constant), the influence of Dark Energy, and the distribution of Dark Matter. Said Professor MÃ¡rio Santos, Principal Investigator of the MeerKLASS survey at the University of the Western Cape:

This is a milestone in establishing 21-cm intensity mapping as a novel tool for cosmology. This measurement took a decade of patient work by researchers spread across seven countries and three continents - and many of them are early-career scientists who have spent their whole career on this project. Such an ambitious result requires sustained and genuine teamwork from many people. And none of it would exist without the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory, which built and operates MeerKAT and helped sort out the many challenges with this survey along the way. It is a reminder that science at this level is a large collaborative effort.

Further Reading: University of Portsmouth

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. #6486. Brick Kilns Became Cleaner and More Profitable, but Workers Saw No Benefits

Bangladesh’s brick kilns found a way to pollute less and earn more, but workers saw no measurable improvement in their pay or working conditions.

Simple adjustments to how coal is fed and bricks are stacked helped traditional kilns burn less fuel, release less pollution, and produce better bricks. Yet a companion study found no measurable improvement in wages, health, child labor, or coercive working conditions during the study period.

The findings expose a gap between improving an industry’s performance and improving life for its workforce. They also suggest that protecting workers requires measures aimed directly at their needs.

The multiyear research effort involved Nina Brooks, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability and a faculty affiliate of its Center for South Asian Studies.

Bangladesh’s rapid urban growth depends on an industry with a substantial environmental footprint. The country is the world’s fourth-largest brick producer, and roughly 8,000 traditional kilns supply more than 90% of its domestic brick consumption. Alongside carbon emissions, the kilns release fine particles known as PM2.5. Ambient air pollution causes 4.9 million premature deaths globally, with South Asia accounting for 32% of them.

Brooks began investigating brickmaking about eight years ago during her doctoral studies. She and her collaborators mapped kilns with satellite imagery and machine learning, studied regulation, and examined health effects in communities downwind. Their work revealed why restricting kiln locations alone could not solve the pollution problem.

“Bangladesh is one of the world’s most densely populated countries,” Brooks said. “It is not feasible to move brick kilns away from all schools, health facilities, and urban centers that may be harmed by the pollution.”

Instead, researchers worked with owners, managers, and workers to improve existing operations. They introduced more continuous coal feeding, brick-stacking arrangements that improved airflow, and measures to reduce heat loss. None required replacing kilns or purchasing major new equipment.

After a small pilot, the team expanded the approach to hundreds of kilns. Results published in Science showed that training and technical support reduced energy use by about 10.5% across kilns assigned to the program. Estimated emissions fell by 171 metric tons (about 188.5 US tons) of carbon dioxide and 0.45 metric tons (about 990 pounds) of PM2.5 per kiln over a firing season.

Among kilns that adopted the practices because of the program, energy use dropped about 23%, while carbon dioxide and PM2.5 emissions each fell roughly 20%. Owners spent less on fuel and produced a greater proportion of higher-quality bricks.

Adoption had increased when researchers returned the next firing season, suggesting the changes had staying power. “Because the changes are economically beneficial for owners, they had a strong incentive to continue following them,” Brooks said.

For businesses facing expensive equipment upgrades and authorities struggling to enforce environmental rules, the findings offered a practical route to cleaner production.

The researchers then examined whether those business benefits reached workers. Bangladesh’s brick industry relies on a large, mostly informal workforce whose employment can involve debt, advance payments, long hours, hazardous conditions, and restrictions on leaving. A companion study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences examined 246 kilns in the Khulna Division and included private interviews with 1,442 workers.

Seventy percent of workers reported having no personal protective equipment, and 71% lacked a formal labor contract. Forty-two percent described restrictions on movement or communication. Across the sample, roughly 20% met the U.S. Department of State’s definitions of labor trafficking. At nearly half the kilns, at least 1 in 6 workers met those definitions.

Adult workers also reported child labor at more than 70% of the kilns, with most reported cases involving children ages 14 to 17.

The intervention lowered fuel costs by 9.6% and improved brick quality by 8.1%, but researchers detected no corresponding improvement in trafficking, child labor, wages, health, or working conditions. Although changes were possible within the study period, the economic gains did not produce measurable benefits for workers.

Higher productivity is often expected to help employees through better pay or conditions. The kiln studies show why that outcome cannot be assumed when coercion and limited bargaining power shape the labor market.

“In many countries, not just Bangladesh, labor laws are hard to enforce, particularly in informal sectors. So, it’s critical to find other ways to protect workers from exploitation,” said Grant Miller, a professor of medicine at Stanford University. “Our study shows that we cannot rely on productivity gains alone to do that, at least not in the short run. Finding approaches that work beyond regulation is a central goal of our ongoing research.”

Expanding the cleaner production program revealed that kiln owners in other regions were more reluctant to adopt the changes. In districts around Dhaka, owners were considerably less likely to adopt the practices than those in Khulna. Yet participating kilns achieved comparable reductions in fuel use and emissions, Brooks said. “So, we’re seeing greater hesitation,” she said. “But once they adopt, we see the same benefits.”

Sameer Maithel, the research team’s lead technical expert, said the reasons are still being investigated. Owners operating on narrow margins may hesitate to change familiar methods while facing unpredictable coal prices, brick demand, and regulation. Differences in kiln size, land, and production practices can also make adoption easier in one location than another.

“Informal brick production in South Asia faces a lot of uncertainty: weather, energy prices, market demand, and regulation all shift unpredictably. Many kiln owners also have limited technical and managerial support, and conditions vary from region to region,” Maithel said. “All of this makes scaling up slow and complex, and it takes sustained, dedicated effort.”

The lack of improvement for workers has prompted the team to test more direct measures. During the most recent brickmaking season, researchers returned to Khulna with recommendations developed through pilot work and conversations with workers.

They recommended masks for people crushing coal, goggles and protective footwear for fire workers, and head protection for brick carriers. Other measures included sanitation and cooking facilities, shaded rest areas, clean water, heat-stress awareness, and information about child labor.

“None of the owners I interviewed objected to improving conditions for workers, though some disagreed with specific components. They saw the cost as negligible compared to what they spend running a kiln. As they put it, if workers do better work because of it, it’s worth doing,” said Mohammad Saeed Munim, a research officer in the Health Systems and Population Studies Division of the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research in Bangladesh.

Researchers had expected more resistance. Owners’ willingness to consider these changes now gives the team an opportunity to test whether targeting workers’ daily needs can deliver improvements that greater productivity alone did not.

“Reducing emissions and air pollution from informal brick kilns: Evidence from Bangladesh” by Nina Brooks, Debashish Biswas, Sameer Maithel, Grant Miller, Aprajit Mahajan, M. Rofi Uddin, Shoeb Ahmed, Moogdho Mahzab, Mahbubur Rahman and Stephen P. Luby, 8 May 2025, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.adr7394

“Productivity gains and work conditions in coercive labor markets: Experimental evidence from the Bangladesh brick sector” by Grant Miller, Debashish Biswas, Aprajit Mahajan, Kimberly Singer Babiarz, Nina Brooks, Jessie Brunner, Sania Ashraf, Jack Shane, Alvise Scarabosio, Sameer Maithel, Shoeb Ahmed, Moogdho Mahzab, Mohammad Rofi Uddin, Mahbubur Rahman and Stephen P. Luby, 16 July 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2528388123

#6485. Highly Specific Observations While Scouting for the 2026 Eater Awards

The great dishes, gorgeous restaurants, and quirky cocktails that commanded our attention, even if they didn’t make the big list

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The past year has been one of “Great Chickenings” and fine dining flips, British food invasions and restaurants whose dining rooms feel like living rooms, vibrant global steakhouses and unserious Y2K food. Among the slate of our 2026 Eater Award winners — which also brought undeniable new chef talent, core-memory-forming dishes, and groundbreaking bakeries and bars — are the places we could not stop thinking about for highly specific reasons. While this crop of restaurants and bars did not make the ultimate cut for the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, they commanded enough attention during our expansive scouting and research months to deserve acknowledgment. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

Cabbage is having its moment. From a star turn on the Sandy Liang runway as a ruffled bag to a hand-painted Bordallo Pinheiro dinner set and a declaration from Vogue that the leafy green has gone “chic,” the cruciferous vegetable is 2026’s “it” girl. The cult of the cabbage has made its way to Monte’s in Montecito, a cozy Korean American bistro where cone cabbage gets coal-roasted and kissed with salty smoked shiitake XO, an umami-heavy spin on the Hong Kong-born sauce. The fall-apart-tender cabbage beds on creamy tofu puree, the whole thing studded with hazelnuts that bring out the vegetable’s innate sweetness. Preparations like the one at Monte’s make it feel as though cabbage isn’t just this year’s distinguished vegetable — its dominance is here to stay. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

Maybe it was the Negroni, the Old Fashioned, and the gingery mezcal-laced Missed Opportunity. Perhaps it was the jetlag (who can say for sure?), but the bathroom at Bobo — the Filipino bar attached to Muhajir in Chicago’s Lincoln Park — left a lasting impression on me. In a world that’s fully embraced the bathroom selfie, Bobo has answered the call with refractory horizontal-mirrored panel walls and colored light that shifts from reds to greens, turning this lavatory into a mesmerizing disco ball. It’s a fitting touch that matches chef Jacob Dela Cruz’s vision for a red-light district-esque tropical hideaway. — Brenna Houck, Eater editorial manager

In a world of outrageous martinis, the one at Greenpoint Malaysian restaurant Kelang earns its playful name. The Dirty Fish riffs on a Vesper with gin, vodka, dry vermouth, and, saliently, fish sauce, which levels up the drink’s savoriness in every way. The pungent condiment mimics olive brine, delivering a salty taste of the sea to the already strong drink, which then gets garnished with wavy scallions and a long sliver of aromatic ginger. The cocktail showcases owner Chris Low’s background as a Malaysian kid who grew up in New York. It’s simply presented — a cloudy drink in a stemmed coupe glass with those gloating garnishes — and pairs best with that fluffy paratha served over creamy and spicy dal. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

Gone may be the days of business power lunches at Wolfgang Puck’s Spago or Grill on the Alley that required a suit and tie. In their place, a new arrangement has emerged — the low-key power lunch. There may be no better place for the midday meal masquerading as a meeting right now than at Little Fish in Melrose Hill, the first full-service restaurant from the former pop-up-turned-fish sandwich window. The light-filled dining room hums during daytime with flexibly scheduled creatives and well-dressed parents toting young children, all adults in the room sipping wine picked by sommelier Kae Whalen. On the menu, a tuna melt from maverick chefs and owners Anna Sonenshein and Niki Vahle will convert even nonbelievers, especially when paired with peppery fries dunked in horseradish aioli. Of course, there is the calling card fried fish sandwich, but smarter diners go for the beach sandwich layered with guindilla peppers and soy-cured mussels and a bay leaf chip stracciatella flecked with chocolate chips. Melrose Hill and its confluence of independent restaurants has morphed into a miniature walkable neighborhood — the perfect place to see and be seen. And what’s more low-key power lunch than that? — RR

Historically, California is a gold mine of kitsch restaurants, from Clifton’s Republic to the pillowy pink dining room at the Madonna Inn. Night Hawk is the next jewel in that camp crown; the Greek-influenced San Diego restaurant is an anchor of Coronado Island’s hypermaximalist new Baby Grand hotel and beckons diners into a lush, faux-rock-filled outdoor dining room with pink clamshell chairs, waterfalls, and cocktails that have names like the Adonis in Bloom and Spanakopita Punch. In short: Tony Duquette by way of an acid tab. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

British food hit a fever pitch nationally this year as Americans awakened to the allure of meat pies and mushy peas. But if any restaurant truly dispelled notions of the country’s cuisine as dull or bland, it was Ambassadors Clubhouse, with its extensive menu of Punjabi showstoppers such as seven-layer, aloo-filed, Amritsari-style samosas; butter chicken in the form of lollipop-like chops with a heady char; and matka Beliram lamb, its crimson oil heralding intense flavor. In opulent, velvet-adorned surroundings that feel like a hideaway from the city, this luxe London import deliciously makes the case that Indian food is as essential to British cuisine as fish and chips. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

The most beautiful new restaurant in California is tucked into a shopping center in Montecito’s tony upper village. Little Mountain, which opened in November 2025 under chef Diego Moya, gives more to the scene than just a locavore menu that leans into live-fire cooking — it brings a bona fide, Architectural Digest-worthy destination that I would get married (and remarried) in. It may be hard to decide which room to sit in should you land a reservation in time: the comfortable dining room with gold-veil natural lighting and plush caramel booths and banquettes; the larger-party table that foregrounds an open kitchen and its centerpiece hearth; the dim, dark bar that may be the sexiest sliver of drinking den on the Central Coast; the covered patio that leads into a monarchial private dining area; or the outdoor patio that evokes dining in a home garden. Anywhere you sit, you can’t go wrong, especially as the food starts landing in front of you. — NF

Chef Theo Adley opened Heretík last spring, and it has brought a breath of fresh, San Sebastián-esque sea breeze air into the Denver dining scene. The French- and Basque-leaning restaurant serves an endless summer menu of dishes like Santa Barbara uni, a playful pan con tomate martini, and scallops à la plancha with bearnaise and seaweed. The menu’s coastal Euro allure gets amplified by its interior design choices, which sprinkle in vintage furniture and tapered, wax drip-laden candles — but with a name like Heretík, you know that all of that romance is going to come with a healthy dose of cheek. — FK

Chickens, you can’t take credit for this one: The British-inspired pub Dean’s proved that bigger is not always better with its take on a Scotch egg, which employs quail eggs instead of the typical chicken ones. In larger Scotch eggs, what appears in each bite can be inconsistent. But the result of the shrunken-down approach here is a reliably favorable ratio of meat to egg, in which each bite at once encompasses crunchy breading, tender meat filling, runny yolk, and just enough still-bouncy egg white. It’s as nonnegotiable at Dean’s as a pint of Guinness. — BM

Ladyfish in Portland, Maine, has been clear about one thing since the beginning: “A summer fling,” the restaurant declared when it announced its May 2026 arrival. Jordan and Marisa Rubin of Portland sushi spot Mr. Tuna convinced chef Christine Lau to relocate from New York City to helm the seasonal seafood pop-up. Lau, whose resume includes Japanese-Italian and Chino Latino restaurants, brings her distinctive flair to classic Maine ingredients for dishes like scallops in a blanket with fried milk bread and the showstopping twin lobster mountain served with fries, rice cakes, and dan dan au poivre sauce. True to its word, the restaurant closed at the end of October. Here’s hoping the return of next year’s summertime crowds also brings back this match made in seafood heaven. — Stephanie Wu, editor in chief

Los Angeles-born chef Ray Garcia opened Broken Spanish Comedor in Culver City in late 2025, years after his groundbreaking Mexican fine dining restaurant, Broken Spanish, and more casual B.S. Taqueria closed in Downtown Los Angeles. Garcia’s contribution to Alta California cuisine, rooted in Mexican cooking told through a California lens, remains one of the most distinct of this generation of restaurants. Still, he manages to surprise both longtime fans and newcomers to his work: The Comedor, whose name nods to the Indigenous homestyle restaurant tradition in Mexico, feels fresh in its A-frame home. It’s not uncommon for locals and those working in Los Angeles hospitality to stop in for a meal of crispy, crown-whorled chicharron or quesillo-threaded refried lentils; a classics-leaning drinks menu (cócteles, cervezas, vino) keeps the room humming happily. In a year brimming with big restaurant comebacks (see also: Venice’s resurrected Tasting Kitchen and Keith Corbin’s reframed Alta Adams), it feels good to have an Angeleno chef like Ray Garcia capture our collective imagination again. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

If ever there was a destination in need of effective hangover cures, it’s New Orleans. While I was totally ready to rally after a two-bar, two-restaurant evening the night before (I am, of course, a professional), I also wasn’t mad about consuming something fortifying at Casimiro, the charming all-day cafe from award-winning Acamaya chef Ana Castro, the next morning. The restaurant delivered: textbook chilaquiles, impossibly fluffy conchas, crispy pescaditos, and one of the best tortas I’ve ever had. If hair of the dog is in your future in the City That Always Drinks, go with the well-balanced Cynar daiquiri to finish. — Missy Frederick, dining editorial director

The weirdest thing I ate on a pastry this year was “lettuce cream” lacquered onto the BLT Danish at Dahlia in Minneapolis. The chartreuse-colored cream anchored a slice of late-August tomato and dollops of bacon jam atop persistently crisp laminated dough. One bite was enough to make me think, This should be more of a thing. You wouldn’t know at first glance that this bakery, tucked into an office complex, turns out treats of this caliber: jam-filled croissants with speculoos crumble, unassumingly perfect English muffins, plush milk bread and fluffy focaccia for sandwiches. This kind of out-of-the-box baking makes eating pastries right now so fun. — BM

#6484. ALMA Reveals a Jet of Cool Gas from a Microquasar

There's a strange gamma-ray emitter in the Large Magellanic Cloud that has astronomers stumped about its source. It lies within the ashes left behind by a supernova that created a compact object that's part of the system. The supernova remnant provides a piece of evidence to explain the emissions, but not the whole story.

So, a research team from two Japanese universities decided to give the object, called LMC P3, a closer look. Instead of tracking the gamma rays, they looked at the object with the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile. This is a series of radio telescopes that provide highly detailed radio views of objects in the sky. ALMA focused on radio emissions from carbon monoxide (CO) molecules in proximity to the cold cloud in the area around LMC P3. It's one of the few such objects found outside the Milky Way, and astronomers have dubbed it a microquasar. It consists of a giant O-type star and a compact object that could be explained by the existence of a black hole or a neutron star.

According to astronomer Yasuo Fukui of Nagoya University, who worked with team leader Bhuvana Gadikere Rajendra of Gifu University, what they detected at LMC P3 is unusual. âWe discovered a gigantic molecular jet,â said Fukui. The jet consists of molecular gas that stretches out across 26 light-years of space. For reference, the bright star Vega lies 25 light-years away from us, so the jet would connect us and that star quite easily.

The strange thing is, the molecular jet itself is cold (by our standards), but astrophysically "heated" to a temperature of about 35 to 60 Kelvin. By comparison, that's warmer than the 15 Kelvin surrounding gas but still very cold. That temperature difference means that the gas is interacting with another jet— this one a high-energy stream of particles coming from the nearby compact object with enough energy to power gamma-ray emissions. The object turns out to be a micro-quasar, which would have the energy to do the job.

Micro-quasars are interesting objects. They actually consist of two objects: a stellar-mass black hole or neutron star coupled with a companion star. The black hole constantly sucks material from the star, and that creates a swirling accretion disk around the black hole. It's a fairly energetic interaction that leads to X-ray and gamma-ray emissions. It also creates high-speed jets that travel out at nearly light-speed velocities. They're called micro-quasars because they're a smaller type of quasar, which is a highly active region around a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy.

Fukui said the relatively high temperature observed over a large fraction of the molecular cloud makes it a very strong case that the gas is interacting with a high-energy jet coming from the compact object â precisely the kind of jet that can also power LMC P3âs gamma rays. This also provides a boost to the idea that the object is a black hole, leftover from the collapse of a supermassive star in a supernova explosion.

Prior to this discovery, scientists had two competing theories about what could be powering the emissions. One is that pulsar winds could have been causing the emissions. That means the object has to be a pulsar, which would send out streams of energetic particles in pulsations as the object spins. Neutron stars are created when a supermassive star collapses, but a stellar remnant remains behind consisting solely of neutrons packed tightly together in a space about the size of a city.

The other theory is that the object is indeed a microquasar. The discovery of the newly found "cold" jet strongly suggests that the compact object could be a stellar-mass black hole or neutron star that draws in material from its companion to form an accretion disk. Since black holes drive more powerful jets than neutron stars, the fact that LMC P3âs gamma-ray emission is particularly high is a smoking gun pointing toward the micro-quasar origin of the signals found by ALMA. âIt provides very strong support for the possibility that its central object is a black hole," said Fukui.

Object LMC P3 was first discovered in 2016 thanks to its very strong gamma-ray emissions. It was also the first one found outside the Milky Way. From the beginning, astronomers suspected it was an X-ray binary, and Chandra X-ray Observatory studies seemed to confirm that. Then, the FERMI telescope observed it and found a 10.3-day period in gamma-ray emissions from the object. That suggested a number of ideas, including jets.

Detailed observations with ALMA focused on the surrounding gas clouds and found the "cold" jet streaming away. That raised questions about the "launch mechanism" for such a jet. In the paper the team published about their observations, they wrote: "We interpret that the high temperatures are due to shock heating of a microquasar jet driven by the gamma-ray binary, where the compact object has an accretion disk fed by the O-star winds. The CO jet matches existing predictions from magnetohydrodynamical simulations, which show that a CO jet can form from the interaction of the microquasar jet and an ambient interstellar medium (ISM) cloud. These results provide strong evidence that CO jets are a signature sculpted by microquasar jets, lending support for mass accretion in LMC P3 as the gamma-ray origin.

This discovery has important astrophysical implications for the study of high-energy emissions and the objects that provide them. Coupled with ongoing studies of such objects as SS 433, which is the first microquasar ever found, discoveries such as LMC P3 give new insight into the actions of compact objects and their interactions with surrounding objects.

Has a Mysterious Gamma-ray Powerhouse Revealed its Smoking Gun?

ALMA Observations of DEM L241/LMC P3 in the Large Magellanic Cloud: Evidence for the Formation of Cool Molecular Jets Driven by a Microquasar

NASA's Swift Observatory went out in a blaze of glory this week, but it left behind millions of images of the universe that could fuel discoveries for decades.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory fell out of space, burning up in the sky over Sumatra. It was a fitting, fiery end for a telescope that spent 22 years studying the most powerful explosions in the universe — and, even with Swift gone, its observations will continue to feed scientific curiosity for years to come.

Swift's most important contributions to astronomy are not exactly eye candy. Designed to swivel toward deep-space explosions at a moment's notice, Swift excelled at capturing bright, fleeting and faraway specks of light. The multiwavelength observatory was equipped with optical, ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray instruments, allowing it to catch cosmic bursts of energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, zeroing in on flares of light that other telescopes might miss.

One of its most significant detections was a gamma-ray burst — an incredibly bright blast, likely emitted by a giant star as it exploded in a supernova before collapsing into a black hole. Swift's famous image of GRB 221009A, or the BOAT ‪—‬ short for "brightest of all time" ‪—‬ looks like a speckled orange bull's-eye, caused by waves from the explosion rippling across space.

How the Swift Observatory saw the gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A, which may be the most energetic emission of this kind ever seen.

But Swift also took millions of observations of the nearby universe, including galaxies in our backyard. One of its most jaw-dropping images is this 24-hour exposure of the Andromeda galaxy (M31), located about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

Andromeda is the closest major galaxy to ours, and it may be destined for a shared fate. Scientists suspect that Andromeda and the Milky Way are drawing closer together and might eventually collide. The merger would add Andromeda's roughly 1 trillion stars to our sky, though there probably wouldn't be any life left on Earth to appreciate it.

In Swift's view of our encroaching neighbor, captured with the observatory's ultraviolet instrument, tens of thousands of Andromeda's stars shine like sapphires set in a sparkling ring.

According to NASA, the observatory detected some 20,000 ultraviolet light sources in this image, captured over two months from May to July 2008. These sources include thousands of dense, hot star clusters scattered across Andromeda's 150,000-light-year-wide ring, as well as the distant galaxy M32 (seen as a bright orb of light to the bottom right of Andromeda's center).

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In visible-light images of Andromeda taken with ground-based telescopes, the galaxy's bright center bleaches out many of the fiery young stars that emerge in Swift's view. While Swift likely won't be remembered best for shimmering starscapes like this one, it's a powerful reminder that looking at familiar structures in a new light can change everything.

#6482. Automated Assembly in Space is the Future and NOM4D is Showing the Way

If we want big things in space, we'll have to build and assemble them there. Rocket fairings are not large enough to accommodate the large things we want to have in space. Not only that, but the stubborn rocket equation refuses to bend itself to our desires.

Telescopes like the JWST feature ingenious folding designs that unfold in space like insects metamorphosizing. That was a very impressive way to bypass the restrictions imposed by rocket fairings. But that's not practical in every case.

What's far more feasible is sending smaller components into space inside fairings and then assembling them into a larger structure once there. That's what NOM4D, the Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials and Mass-efficient Design program is demonstrating. NOM4D reached an important milestone recently when it successfully demonstrated automated in-space assembly for the first time.

The demonstration involved a gantry robot, also known as a linear robot, building a typical truss structure. Gantry robots move in straight lines along x, y, and z axes. The payload came from Caltech and consisted of individual components with custom joints put together to form the structure. The individual components were not only assembled, but a thin reflective mesh that mimics what a space-based antenna might have was also simultaneously applied.

âNOM4Dâs objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space,â said Andrew Detor, NOM4D program manager. âBy âvery large,â I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today.â

This concept image shows a space-based antenna autonomously assembled by a NOM4D-type device. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

There is no shortage of ideas of how space-based manufacturing and construction could be used, but it all starts with programs like NOM4D. NOM4D is fairly simple at this point, like a child's construction toy, but that's its strength.

âYou can think of the Caltech approach as similar to Tinkertoys or Kânex construction toys: individual truss members are joined at nodes, one section at a time, to create a larger structure,â Detor said. âWithin the automated assembly box, each section is built piece by piece, a reflective mesh is attached, and the assembled sections are deployed as they are complete. There are no complicated robotics or advanced algorithms; itâs just solid engineering from the Caltech team to combine operations in a way that scales.â

Decades ago, thinkers proposed different types of rotating space stations that could be homes for thousands of people. The O'Neill Cylinder is probably the most well-known one of these, and space-heads and sci-fi dreamers of a certain age may have carried around a dog-eared copy of Gerard K. O'Neill's "The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space."

"More important than material issues, I think there is reason to hope that the opening of a new, high frontier will challenge the best that is in us, that the new lands waiting to be built in space will give us new freedom to search for better governments, social systems, and ways of life, and that our children may thereby find a world richer in opportunity by our efforts during the decades ahead," O'Neill wrote.

The O'Neill Cylinder lies in the realm of science fiction or the distant future for now, as do O'Neill's hopes for humanity. But that was 50 years ago, and technology has advanced considerably, even if how humans conduct themselves hasn't advanced at the same pace.

But there are other proposed space structures that are closer to reality, and they may be stages towards O'Neill's hopeful vision that can be built by NOM4D or its successor.

It may begin with Low-Earth Orbit transfer stations and lunar orbit stations that would expand our presence in space. The proposed Lunar Gateway was one of these, and was envisioned as a modular design built in space from pre-made components. It would be a docking station and communications relay facility for trips to the lunar surface and operations there. These types of orbital facilities could be hybrids of pre-made components and structural frameworks made by NOM4D or something like it.

This concept image shows how a NOM4D-inspired device might autonomously construct a circular truss structure in space. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

Another future use for scalable construction concerns lunar lava tubes. The Moon has what appear to be networks of subsurface lava tubes that provide natural protection from hazards. Robotic assembly could feasibly be used to reinforce these natural tubes and turn them into habitats.

Another idea is liquid mirror telescopes. Building a huge telescope mirror and sending it into space would be near impossible, but a liquid mirror telescope could be built in a lunar crater out of components shipped individually into space. And NASA's Lunar Crater Radio Telescope (LCRT) is a concept for a crater-based telescope on the lunar far side, isolated from Earth's radio pollution. These ideas are waiting for the engineering to catch up.

âIn a future space economy, weâre going to need large things,â Detor said. âThink large space depots or habitats, large solar arrays to collect power, or large radio antennas to explore the edges of the universe. Those things require size, and NOM4D gives us a path to accelerate creation of new capabilities.â

The rapid advancement of the NOM4D program surprised even NOM4D personnel themselves. This successful on-orbit demonstration wasn't expected to happen so soon.

Back in February 2025, NOM4D changed its timeline. What was expected to be a third phase of more laboratory tests was instead changed to on-orbit tests, and SpaceX launched Caltech's NOM4D payload into space in March 2026.

âCaltech [California Institute of Technology] and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have demonstrated tremendous advances in the first two phases and have now partnered in Phase 3 with space-launch companies to conduct in-space testing of their novel assembly processes and materials,â Detor said at the time. âOriginally, Phase 3 was going to be about making things more precisely in the lab than we did in Phase 2. But we said, âYou know, the maturity is there, and there would be more impact if we took the capabilities we have now and actually go demonstrate them in space to show that it can be done,â"Detor said.

Now, way ahead of its original schedule, NOM4D has demonstrated its capabilities and is maturing rapidly. As Detor makes clear, leaping from the laboratory to space is a huge jump.

âItâs the speed and the scale that made this a DARPA project. We went from the idea of an on-orbit demo to launching a working prototype into space in 15 months,â Detor said. âOperating in space is much harder than operating on the ground â thereâs virtually no margin to address issues that may arise. Testing in the operational environment is instrumental to rapidly maturing the technology.â

There's still another test upcoming for NOM4D now that it's demonstrated successful on-orbit assembly. Next, the NOM4D team from University of Illinois Urbana-Champagne will launch a test project to the ISS. This will be more than just assembly; it will demonstrate composite material processing. A monomer resin will be used to build a high-strength structure in space. It will use an energy-efficient method to heat the resin and create a strong polymer. This is similar to how resins are used in Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) manufacturing to build things like aerospace components, where strength and light weight are critical.

If that test is successful, then it really will be time to start thinking big, according to Detor.

This concept image shows what the future of NOM4D-like construction might look like. Large space structures like these could be built entirely in space. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz

âThe NOM4D Caltech demonstration is not an endpoint; itâs a beginning,â Detor said. âNow that weâve demonstrated a process that can scale to large structures, what do we go make? What wild ideas get assembled thousands of miles above us and what new capabilities do those structures enable?â

Is it time to open Gerard K. O'Neill's seminal book again?

The O'Neill Cylinder, the OG of space habitats. Maybe one day. Image Credit: By NASA/Rick Guidice - https://space.nss.org/settlement/nasa/70sArtHiRes/70sArt/art.html (image link), Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=675434
