КОНЦЕПЦИЯ ИССЛЕДОВАНИЯ РАЗРЕЖЕННЫХ ПОТОКОВ ВОДОРОДА: СИНТЕЗ КВАНТОВО-ГРАВИТАЦИОННЫХ И ВРЕМЕННЫХ АСПЕКТОВ

Аннотация. Настоящая работа посвящена исследованию разреженных потоков водорода, играющих ключевую роль в эволюции Вселенной и представляющих собой протяженные структуры из нейтрального и ионизированного водорода, связывающие галактики. В статье рассматриваются теоретические и наблюдательные аспекты изучения данных потоков, опирающиеся на пионерские работы в области космической электродинамики, квантовой механики и космологии. Автором представлен обзор современных исследований, выявивших сложную нитевидную структуру водородных облаков и подчеркивающих многокомпонентный характер взаимодействия различных физических процессов в разреженных потоках. В рамках исследования выдвинута концепция «Спирали Бытия», объясняющая формирование рукавов галактик, и постулируется концепция «Галактических связей», предполагающая существование межгалактических потоков вещества. Акцентируется внимание на роли гравитационного взаимодействия в формировании структуры разреженных потоков и необходимости комплексного изучения их характеристик. Предлагаемый подход позволяет объединить различные научные направления для дальнейшего исследования данной области.

Ключевые слова: водород, разреженные потоки водорода, межгалактическая среда, эволюция галактик, межзвездный газ, гравитация

Сегодня научные наблюдения за космическим пространством открывают перед нами удивительные картины: галактики, звездные скопления, облака газа и пыли, простирающиеся на огромные расстояния. Среди этих объектов особое место занимают разреженные потоки водорода, которые, как тонкие нити, связывают галактики между собой. Данные потоки, состоящие из нейтрального и ионизированного водорода, играют важную роль в эволюции Вселенной, являясь резервуаром вещества для формирования новых звезд и галактик. Изучение их свойств и динамики представляет собой сложную и актуальную задачу современной астрофизики и общей теоретической физики. В рамках настоящего исследования для начала определим значение и особенности разреженных потоков водорода, которые требуют тщательного анализа существующих исследований и научных подходов. Разреженные потоки водорода – это протяженные структуры, состоящие преимущественно из атомов водорода, с плотностью значительно ниже, чем в галактиках или межзвездных облаках. Они могут существовать как в нейтральной, так и в ионизированной форме, и отличаются большим разнообразием по своим размерам, плотности и кинематическим свойствам [1]. Исследования разреженных потоков водорода представляет собой междисциплинарную проблему, находящуюся на стыке квантовой механики, астрофизики и теории гравитации. Пионерские работы Х. Альфвена [2] по космической электродинамике заложили основы понимания поведения плазмы в галактических магнитных полях. Дальнейшее развитие этих идей было продолжено в работах С. Чандрасекара [3], исследовавшего устойчивость гидродинамических течений в условиях звездной эволюции. Квантово-механические аспекты поведения атомарного водорода были детально изучены П. Дираком [4] и Р. Фейнманом [5], разработавшими математический аппарат для описания спиновых взаимодействий. Современные исследования межзвездной среды, проведенные с использованием телескопа ALMA [6] и космической обсерватории «Хаббл» [7], выявили сложную нитевидную структуру водородных облаков, требующую пересмотра традиционных моделей. Теоретические работы Р. Пенроуза [8] по квантовой гравитации и С. Хокинга [9] по физике черных дыр предоставили важные научные теории для понимания поведения материи в экстремальных гравитационных полях. Особого внимания заслуживают работы А. Линде [10] по инфляционной космологии и В. Муханова [11] по теории квантовых флуктуаций, позволившие по-новому взглянуть на процессы структурообразования во Вселенной. Одним из основоположников исследований межгалактической среды и, в частности, разреженных потоков водорода, является Яков Борисович Зельдович [12]. Его работы по космологии и теории крупномасштабной структуры Вселенной заложили фундамент для понимания процессов формирования и эволюции этих потоков. Зельдович предложил концепцию «космической паутины», в которой галактики и их скопления расположены вдоль нитей и узлов, образованных гравитационной нестабильностью в ранней Вселенной [13]. Разреженные потоки водорода, таким образом, являются частью этой космической паутины. Также существенный вклад в изучение нейтрального водорода (HI) в межгалактической среде внесли работы Дж. Верк [14]. С помощью радиоастрономических наблюдений она и ее коллеги исследовали распределение HI в окрестностях галактик и обнаружили протяженные облака и потоки нейтрального водорода, связанные с галактиками. Эти наблюдения показали, что галактики не являются изолированными островами во Вселенной, а взаимодействуют со своим окружением посредством обмена веществом [15]. При этом математическое моделирование разреженных потоков водорода требует учета множества физических процессов, таких как гравитация, гидродинамика, радиационные процессы и химические реакции. Одним из первых исследователей, разработавших численные модели формирования галактик и межгалактической среды, был А.А. Курбатов [16]. Его работы по численному моделированию космологической эволюции позволили проследить за образованием крупномасштабной структуры Вселенной и, в частности, за формированием разреженных потоков водорода [17]. В последние годы большой интерес вызывает изучение ионизированного водорода (HII) в межгалактической среде. Например, исследования Р. Малхотры [18] показали, что HII может составлять значительную часть межгалактического вещества, особенно в окрестностях активных галактических ядер и квазаров. Малхотра и ее коллеги разработали модели ионизации межгалактической среды, учитывающие вклад различных источников излучения. Важным аспектом изучения разреженных потоков водорода является анализ их химического состава. Так, работы К. МакКи [19] были посвящены исследованию образования молекул в межзвездной и межгалактической среде. Автор разработал модели химической эволюции потоков газа, учитывающие процессы ионизации, диссоциации и рекомбинации. Исследования В.В. Ласукова [20] внесли большой вклад в понимание влияние гравитационных сил разного направления на структуру вселенной, которые формируют направление движения потоков в разреженной среде. Работы Широкова В.В. [21] показывают зависимость поляризации от плотности потока, опираясь на его исследования можно выстроить зависимости для описания поведения разреженных потоков. Помимо вышеупомянутых ученых, важный вклад в изучение разреженных потоков водорода внесли Брюс Дрейн [22], чьи работы по физике межзвездной и межгалактической среды являются классическими, а также В. Спринглера [23], разработавший мощные численные методы для моделирования космологической эволюции. В целом, современные исследования подчеркивают комплексный характер взаимодействия различных физических процессов в разреженных потоках водорода, что требует дальнейшего развития моделей и подходов, объединяющих астрофизику, плазменную физику, квантовую механику и космологию. Таким образом, исследование разреженных потоков водорода затрагивает широкий спектр вопросов, требующих комплексного подхода, объединяющего наблюдательные данные, теоретические модели и численное моделирование. Синхронизация вращательных движений атомов водорода, влияние гравитационных полей на этот процесс и изучение временных характеристик синхронизированных состояний представляют собой сложную задачу, требующую учета как квантовых, так и классических эффектов. Анализ влияния гравитационных полей на процесс синхронизации может пролить свет на роль крупномасштабной структуры Вселенной в формировании когерентных состояний [24]. Изучение временных характеристик синхронизированных состояний позволит понять, как долго сохраняется синхронизация и какие факторы влияют на ее разрушение. В дополнение к этому, стоит проанализировать особенности поляризации при различных плотностях потока, связь поляризации со степенью ионизации водорода, влиянием магнитных полей и температуры. Отдельного внимания заслуживает взаимосвязь поляризации с квантовыми состояниями, например, в виде селективного возбуждения определенных энергетических уровней атомов водорода. Исследование собственного времени системы, связи температурных параметров с временными характеристиками, а также влияния инерции на динамику временных процессов играют важную роль. Здесь поможет понимание того, как время течет для частиц, находящихся в разреженных потоках водорода. Связь температурных параметров с временными характеристиками может быть обусловлена тем, что температура является мерой кинетической энергии частиц, а кинетическая энергия, в свою очередь, влияет на скорость течения времени. Понимание этих процессов позволит лучше понять динамику разреженных потоков и их роль в эволюции Вселенной. В процессе исследования разреженных потоков водорода, нами была выдвинута концепция, названная «Спираль Бытия». Она исходит из представления, что сверхновая, при коллапсе, сбрасывает плазму высокой температуры, которая создает магнитное поле вследствие содержания тяжелых частиц. Эта плазма, выброшенная сверхновой, при расширении и охлаждении формирует потоки вещества, которые обогащены тяжелыми элементами. Происходящая здесь синхронизация частиц, на мой взгляд, может быть причиной формирования рукавов галактик. Этот процесс тесно связан с рассмотренными направлениями исследований, позволяя увязать в единую картину макро– и микроскопические процессы во Вселенной. Более того, взрывное расширение при сбросе оболочки из плазмы может приводить к обратному удару по звезде, доводя ее до коллапса и образования черной дыры. Облака газа, падающие на черную дыру, способны к образованию потоков вещества, выбрасываемых из окрестностей черной дыры в виде джетов. Для понимания этих процессов необходимо изучать, как гравитационные, так и гидродинамические силы, действующие в окрестностях черной дыры. Важным моментом является необходимость учитывать собственное время плазмы при переходе от температуры, как состояния массы во времени, к скорости, как состоянии массы в пространстве. Изучение разреженных потоков водорода, как систем в состоянии далёком от равновесия, с большими градиентами температуры и плотности, предоставляют уникальную возможность для изучения этого эффекта, не забывая про релятивистские эффекты, значимые при высоких скоростях движения частиц. Также в рамках проведенного исследования нами постулируется концепция так называемых «Галактических связей», в рамках которой предполагается существование межгалактических структур, представляющих собой светящиеся протяженные образования межзвездного газа, преимущественно состоящего из водорода. Данные структуры рассматриваются как примеры разреженных потоков, осуществляющих гравитационное взаимодействие между галактиками и обеспечивающих перенос вещества. Представляется необходимым проведение комплексного исследования характеристик вышеупомянутых структур, включая определение плотности, температурного режима, химического состава и поляризационных свойств, с целью установления их генезиса и роли в процессах эволюции галактик. Автором статьи акцентируется внимание на гравитационном взаимодействии атомов водорода. Несмотря на малую величину гравитационной силы, её постоянство и всеобщий характер обусловливают её значительное влияние на формирование структуры разреженных потоков. Анализ баланса сил, действующих на атомы водорода в рассматриваемых потоках, позволит получить информацию о механизмах их формирования и дальнейшей эволюции. Также подчеркивается значимость межзвёздного газа, состоящего в основном из водорода, для процессов звёздообразования. Звёзды, аккрецируя межзвёздную среду, обогащаются веществом, высвобождая энергию в виде излучения. Таким образом, детальное изучение свойств разреженных потоков водорода позволит углубить понимание процессов формирования звёзд и их взаимодействия с окружающей средой, включая аккрецию и звёздный ветер. В заключение необходимо отметить, что предложенная концепция исследования разреженных потоков водорода позволяет объединить различные взгляды и подходы, создавая основу для дальнейших исследований. Авторская концепция имеет потенциал для разработки новых методов управления потоками вещества, создания инновационных технологий на основе синхронизированных систем, применения в космической отрасли для изучения межзвёздной среды и развития фундаментальной физики в области квантовых процессов, приближаясь к созданию полной картины эволюции Вселенной.

#6470. The Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields are Very Strange Compared to Earth's

Most planets appear to have magnetic fields, even if they're only weak, remnant fields. Earth has a strong field generated by its internal geodynamo. The other rocky planets have magnetic fields of varying strengths, with the possible exception of Venus. The outer gas planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, all have strong dynamos.

But the magnetic fields generated by the ice giants Uranus and Neptune have some strange properties.

Earth's molten core and internal convection generate its magnetic fields. But the ice giants' magnetic fields are likely generated by fluids that are electrically conductive. These are water, ammonia, and methane ices under extreme pressure and temperatures that alter them and turn them into ionic and superionic phases. Not only is their electrical conductivity at play, but so is convection and the planets' rotations.

But beyond what generates them, they also have other differences. Earth's magnetic field has well-defined north and south poles that drift a little over time, and even flip every couple of hundred thousand years or so. But Voyager 2 showed us how different Uranus and Neptune are. Their fields are in disarray compared to Earth's. They're tilted and multi-peaked.

Uranus' magnetic field doesn't originate in its center, and is tilted almost 60 degrees from its axis of rotation. It's overall geometry is strange, and the magnetic field across its surface is asymmetrical in strength.

Neptune's magnetic field is similarly strange, but weaker. Like Uranus' it's tilted from its rotational axis, by about 47 degrees. It's also offset from the planet's physical center like Uranus'.

The most critical difference between the magnetic fields of Earth and those of Uranus and Neptune is that the fields around the ice giants experience shorter-term variability. In short, they're a weird mess.

While planetary scientists know that these fields are generated inside the planets, they've had to make some guesses as to why they're so strange. New research in Nature Communications Physics has made some progress understanding the pair of ice giants and their strange magnetic fields. It's titled "Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune," and the lead author is Chi Yan. Yan is a research associate at the University of Texax Jackson School of Geosciences.

"Uranus and Neptune exhibit magnetic fields that are non-dipolar and non-axisymmetric, unlike those of any other known planet," the researchers write. "These fields are generated by fluid motions in electrically conducting planetary interiors via dynamo action, offering a window into otherwise inaccessible deep processes."

As we often say at Universe Today, understanding the oddballs and outliers in a group of objects sheds light on how processes operate across the broader group they're a part of. This is true of the ice giants and their magnetic fields. "Understanding why Uranus and Neptune have such unusual magnetic fields provides critical insight into dynamo processes across planets and stars," the authors explain.

This work is based on modelled dynamos that are controlled by interior composition and temperature. They assumed that electrical conductivity increases with depth. The authors say they "produce large-scale magnetic features consistent with the observed fields of Uranus and Neptune..."

This schematic shows the different interior layouts used in the models. a through c show radially variable electrical conductivity profiles for dynamo models with convective shell geometries. d through f show the associated shell geometry for each of a through c. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

âDeep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high,â lead author Yan said in a press release. âUnder these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.â

Voyager 2 gave us our only good close-up look at Uranus and Neptune. It likely caught those fields in a snapshot in time, and the model shows both planets' magnetic fields could shift and change markedly in only decades. The fields are most likely configured much differently than when Voyager 2 visited. This is much different than on Earth, where the magnetic north pole drifts between about 5 and 60 km per year, or about one degree every few decades.

"These non-dipolar dynamos exhibit substantial temporal variation, although the rate fluctuates and can be transiently slow," the authors write. They explain that changes in both intensity and orientation are a possibility in the decades since Voyager 2 flew past Uranus and Neptune, "though the extent of any such variation remains poorly constrained observationally as each planet has been measured in situ only once."

âEarthâs magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years,â said Yan. âOur models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.â

This figure compares observations of Uranus' and Neptune's surface magnetic fields with the fields from models. The figure "demonstrates that the most Uranus-like snapshot from Model 6 (panel c) and the most Neptune-like snapshot from Model 11 (panel d) can change substantially on decadal timescales, with their close morphological resemblance to the respective observed fields (panels a and b) deteriorating markedly after 32 years (panels e and f)," the authors explain. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

"We demonstrate that dynamo models incorporating an electrical conductivity that increases with depth can promote non-dipolar, non-axisymmetric magnetic fields," the authors write, including the M1 peak observed at Uranus and Neptune.

The M1 peak is an important, maybe the most important part, of Voyager 2's magnetic field observations. M=1 represents the lop-sided parts of a magnetic field. On Earth and other planets like Jupiter and Saturn, the magnetic field's power is dominated by symmetric or M=0 components. So for those planets, the M-1 components are at least an order of magnitude weaker than their M-0 components.

But that's not true on Uranus and Neptune. They show a stark contrast. They both have a very strong M-1 peak, the part that represents asymmetric fields. This means that they have dipoles, quadrupoles, and octupoles that are messy and skewed from the axis of rotation.

"Despite current observational and computational limitations, our results indicate that ice-giant-like dynamos can, in some intervals, undergo substantial magnetic field variations on decadal timescales that, if confirmed by future in situ or auroral measurements, could have significant impacts on the surrounding planetary magnetospheres," the authors write.

The JWST has observed the ice giant aurorae and the charged particles involved. These particles respond to the magnetic fields, and those observations could confirm if the magnetic fields have indeed shifted since Voyager 2 visited. Researchers are still working on those observations.

The image on the left is an enhanced-color image of Neptune from NASAâs Hubble Space Telescope. On the right, that image is combined with data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. The cyan splotches are auroral activity captured with the JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec). Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Heidi Hammel (AURA), Henrik Melin (Northumbria University), Leigh Fletcher (University of Leicester), Stefanie Milam (NASA-GSFC)

âWe are busy working on whatâs contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone,â said Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign.

The researchers will combine the JWST data with their models and data from Voyager 2 and take their results as far as they can to try to determine the state of the magnetic fields today. But they're up against some limitations, limitations that can only be lifted by another mission to the ice giants.

There are no firm plans for a mission to the ice giants, but there are concepts. One is NASA's Uranus Orbiter & Probe that would study the planet and its moons, and even send a probe into Uranus' atmosphere. The Neptune Odyssey is another NASA concept. It would also consist of an orbiter and an atmospheric probe. The science community has recognized the importance of these missions, but they're just concepts at this point.

This research may extend to the issue of habitability, though probably only tangentially. Uranus' four major moons could all potentially have subsurface oceans under icy covers, though this is far from confirmed. If they do, then Uranus' magnetic field and related radiation belts could affect these bodies of water, their longevity, and their potential habitability.

Neuroscientists say people can be "trained" to recognize when they're dreaming — in other words, lucid dreaming may be an acquirable skill.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During dreams, bizarre scenes you encounter can seem as tangible as reality; you feel as though you're really flying through the sky or being chased through a jungle of bright-purple trees. But in special cases, people realize they're in the midst of a dream as it's unfolding.

Called lucid dreaming, this phenomenon occurs when we suddenly regain our capacity for metacognition, or thinking about our own thoughts, in the middle of a dream. Lucid dreamers can sometimes even control the content or trajectory of their dreams. Now, researchers claim that they've found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they're awake.

In a study involving a few dozen participants, the scientists found that repeating this training twice a week for a month significantly increased how often participants experienced lucid dreaming. They say the approach could have practical applications as an intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder — but those applications are theoretical, for now.

If you could learn how to lucid dream, would you? Let us know in the poll below, and add your thoughts in the comments.

#6467. Scientists Discover That Male and Female Hearts Age in Surprisingly Different Ways

The heart may age very differently from one region to another. A detailed study of mouse hearts found that molecular signs associated with chronic inflammation and tissue scarring were concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root, rather than being distributed evenly throughout the organ.

Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) identified these hotspots by mapping thousands of cells from young and aged mice. Published in Aging Cell, the findings suggest that structures often overlooked in cardiac aging research may play a central role in how the heart changes over time.

Previous studies of cardiac aging have largely concentrated on heart muscle, particularly the left ventricle, which pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and throughout the body. Because mammalian heart muscle cells have very limited capacity for regeneration, understanding how they deteriorate with age has been a major research priority. The JAX team instead examined the entire heart, using single-cell and spatial genomics technologies to identify both the molecular activity of individual cells and their locations within the organ.

“The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine,” said study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. “It turns out they’re home to many of the cells we’re interested in, and that’s where some of the most important aging-related signals were concentrated.”

“Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue,” Rosenthal said. “We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don’t age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don’t age at the same rate either, even within one individual.”

Aging is associated with persistent, low-grade inflammation, sometimes called “inflammaging.” The researchers focused on two cell populations involved in this process: immune cells that help regulate inflammation (macrophages) and structural cells responsible for maintaining connective tissue and producing scar tissue (fibroblasts). In older mouse hearts, macrophages showed increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and tissue remodeling, while fibroblasts exhibited molecular patterns linked to fibrosis (or scarring).

“To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life,” Rosenthal said. “What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging.”

The team also detected increased activity in two genes within the identified hotspots. Ccl8 produces an inflammatory signaling molecule, while Cdkn1a (also known as p21) helps regulate the cell cycle and is commonly associated with cellular senescence. Their activity points to changes in signaling between neighboring cells, not simply isolated changes within individual cell types. “We’re not talking about single genes. We’re talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts,” Rosenthal said.

Some molecular markers traditionally associated with senescent cells were already present in young mouse hearts. Cellular senescence occurs when cells permanently stop dividing, often following stress or damage. Senescent cells can contribute to inflammation and tissue deterioration, but the researchers found that the presence of commonly used senescence markers does not necessarily establish that a cell has entered this state.

“What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren’t where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us,” Rosenthal said. “That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don’t mean a cell is senescent. There’s nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart.”

The study also identified differences in how fibroblasts responded to aging in male and female mice. In males, older fibroblasts showed greater involvement in molecular pathways associated with fibrosis. In females, aging was linked more closely to pathways involved in heart development and protein production. These findings describe differences in gene activity, not demonstrated differences in cardiac function or disease risk.

Rosenthal noted that cardiovascular disease patterns also differ between men and women, with disease risk generally increasing after menopause in women. However, the mouse findings do not establish a mechanism for those human differences. Comparisons with previously published human heart data did identify several shared molecular programs associated with aging, including pathways involved in cellular stress responses.

“Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process,” said study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.

Age is the leading risk factor for cardiovascular disease, but separating changes caused by aging itself from those associated with lifestyle, environmental exposures, and disease remains difficult. Although the study did not establish whether the identified cellular changes directly impair heart function, the controlled conditions in which the mice lived helped researchers examine the biological effects of aging.

“Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the big questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself,” said study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. “Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta.”

The researchers are now investigating how exercise, diet, and disease influence the interactions between immune cells and fibroblasts. Their goal is to distinguish changes that occur during normal aging from those that may increase the heart’s susceptibility to disease. Although the current findings do not immediately suggest new treatments, the cellular map provides a foundation for studying how inflammation and fibrosis develop in specific regions of the aging heart.

Reference: “Alterations in the Immune-Fibrotic Axis Are Spatially Localized in the Aging Heart” by Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, Amalia Sintou, Yue Zhao, Antonios Somarakis, Harshpreet Chandok, Juliana Alcoforado Diniz, Ramalakshmi Ramasamy, Gretchen T. Clark, Leon Frommer, Sikander Hayat, Brian S. White, Paul Robson, Ron Korstanje, J. Matthew Mahoney and Nadia A. Rosenthal, 5 November 2026, Aging Cell. DOI: 10.1111/acel.70768

This work was supported by the NIH Common Fund through The Jackson Laboratory Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (JAX-Sen TMC U54 AG079753), with additional support from JAX’s National Cancer Institute-designated Cancer Center (P30 CA034196).

#6466. Astrophysicists Want to Forecast When a Black Hole Launches Its Jets

Black holes are not just objects. Some astrophysicists prefer to call them locations. From this vantage point, they're locations where the Universe's laws of physics are pushed to their extreme limits.

Black holes are gravitational gluttons that draw everything in their vicinity towards them. When another star strays too close, the black hole can strip its gas away. The gas doesn't necessarily disappear over the event horizon and leave our observable Universe. It first gathers in a rapidly rotating accretion disk, where its temperature is raised to extreme levels. Some of this superheated material is ejected in a pair of collimated jets from the black hole's axis of rotation.

These jets are streams of plasma and particles that can reach relativistic speeds. They can have an enormous reach; the largest ones come from supermassive black holes and can extend for millions of parsecs into space. Though astrophysicists have witnessed many of these jets, their exact causes remain uncertain. The extreme gravity, magnetic fields, and temperatures around black holes is all a part of it.

Astrophysical jets shape their surroundings by heating star forming gas and moving it around on a massive scale. Stars form from cool gas, and the energy from jets works directly against that. The jets can also inflate bubbles where gas is too diffuse to collapse and form stars.

This JWST NIRCam image shows the jets coming from Messier 87, one of the most massive galaxies in the local Universe. These jets aren't from an x-ray binary, they're from its central SMBH that has billions of solar masses. It's an example of extreme astrophysical jets and an indicator of the extreme physics at black holes. Image Credit: Jan RÃ¶der, Maciek Wielgus et al., Astronomy & Astrophysics (2025)

Astrophysicists want to be able to predict when these jets are triggered so they can quickly gather follow-up observations, and new research in The Astrophysical Journal has made some progress. It's titled "Jet Forecast: Timing of Discrete Jet Ejections of Stellar-mass Black Holes Anticipated via X-Ray Properties," and the authors are Toshihiro Kawaguchi and Kazutaka Yamaoka. Kawaguchi is from the Graduate School of Science and Engineering at the University of Toyama, and Yamaoka is from the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University.

The pair of researchers have been working on this problem for a while. In a 2025 study, they examined an x-ray binary consisting of a black hole and a donor star and found a link between the parameters of the inner accretion disk and jet activity. That research suggested that as the accretion disk's inner edge shrank towards its innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), the black hole launched its jets. "This fact suggests that the jet materials originate from accreting matter from the innermost part of the disk," the authors wrote.

That was progress, but in that paper the researchers pointed out that more observations were needed. "Both X-ray spectral and timing observations are very important to understand the accretion disk states which can change very rapidly. Dense, simultaneous coverage with radio observations are also crucial to understand diskâjet interactions," the authors wrote in the conclusion to their 2025 paper.

This illustration is representative of XTE J1859+226, the system the authors studied in their 2025 paper. It shows a black hole not only drawing material away from the donor star, but also stretching the star into a distorted shape. Image Credit: J. M. Corral-Santana/Corral-Santana et al. 2011 MNRAS

Their 2025 paper was based on observations of a single black hole x-ray binary gathered during an outburst in 1999â2000. This work is based on observations of four black hole binary systems: one from the 2025 paper and three new ones.

There seem to be changes in an x-ray binary's (XRB) x-ray emissions prior to jets being launched. The spectrum is altered, and variability decreases. Astrophysicists have interpreted these changes as a signal that jets are about to be emitted. But the signals haven't been clear and reliable enough, so astrophysicists haven't been able to use them to time their follow-up observations. The researchers' previous work showed that as an accretion disk's inner edge shrank down to its ISCO, jets were launched. This could be the reliable signal astrophysicists are searching for.

This work expands their observations to more XRBs to see if this holds true. The researchers hope to develop a forecasting model for XRB jet launching so that more complete observations can be obtained.

The results show that the rapidly decreasing radius of the inner disk, called Rin, combined with a decrease in x-ray emission variability (indicated by rms), are a reliable predictor of jet launching. "All the four sources turned out to show the precursors of jet ejections (drops in Rin and rms) 1â10 days before radio activities," the authors write.

This artistâs depiction of a jet ejection shows how the jet from the black hole turns on when the inner radius of the accretion disk shrinks down to the ISCO fast enough. Image Credit: Professor Toshihiro Kawaguchi from University of Toyama, Japan and Dr. Kazutaka Yamaoka from Nagoya University, Japan.

They also found that there are no reliably detected increases in the amount of mass accreted prior to the launching of jets. "They show no huge jumps in M prior to each jet ejection," the researchers explain.

In at least one of the XRBs, that rate actually decayed in the 30 days leading up to jet launching. "We examined the time evolution of the accretion rate M of XTE J1859. It turned out to be exponentially decaying during the outburst (with an e-folding timescale of â¼30 days), and shows no huge jumps around the jet ejections," they write.

But XTE J1859 did show a tantalizing hint of enhancement. "There is a hint of â¼20% enhancement in M just before the jet productions," the authors write.

But that's just a hint, and better observations are needed to support it. "Such fine structures in the time evolution of M will be examined by the better data via the âjet forecastâ in the future," the researchers write.

Another notable finding concerns the Eddington limit. It's a theoretical threshold balanced between the inward force of gravity and the outward force of radiation. In two of the four systems, jets formed below this threshold. Some models of jet ejection say that super-Eddington accretion beyond this limit is necessary to launch jets, but these results say otherwise.

âMonitoring of Rin seems to be suitable for predicting the timing of jet ejections,â said Prof. Kawaguchi. âThe development of a âjet forecastâ would enable us to concentrate observing facilities on the expected timing of jet ejections, thereby accelerating our understanding of jet physics.â

Their jet forecasting model would be based on shrinking Rin and X-ray variability, and when both are detected, alerts would be sent out to other telescopes for more complete observations. Those observation would hopefully reveal some more of the extreme physics that dominate and define black holes.

"When both Rin and rms continuously decrease and when Rin is about to reach the ISCO, alerts can be circulated as a âjet forecastâ for triggering ToO (Target of Opportunity) observations," the authors write.

This is more than just purely academic. Earth has been subjected to bombardment by high-energy particles throughout its history. The Earth's protective magnetic shield deflects most of them, but some get through and trigger showers of secondary particles. Convincing evidence is thin, but some researchers still consider them a factor in the course of life on Earth.

âJet ejections in the Universe produce high-energy photons and particles, such as neutrinos, and such cosmic rays have long influenced the evolution of living creatures on Earth, including human beings,â concluded Prof. Kawaguchi.

#6465. A Remote Island Holds a Major Warning Sign for the Future of Humanity

A 180-year accidental experiment on a barren volcanic rock could show us how to reverse deserts—or how to break nature.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The word “terraforming” is typically reserved for discussions of other worlds. Sci-fi writers dream up vast galactic empires where humans have bent entire planetary ecosystems to their will while, in the real world, the world’s richest man contemplates a similar future. But on the remote island of Ascension in the South Atlantic, an accidental 180-year-long experiment shows what happens when you terraform our own planet. Some see the story as a small slice of hope for areas around the world facing desertification in the face of climate change, while others see the history of Ascension Island as a warning about humanity’s impact on the natural world.

Around one million years ago, volcanic eruptions along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge pushed the island up out of the Atlantic. It went unseen by humans until 1501, when Portuguese admiral João da Nova came across it. Two years later, Portuguese navigator Afonso de Albuquerque found it again on the Christian holiday of Ascension Day, which is how the island got its name. However, neither of these expeditions set up shop on the island, and it wasn’t until 1815 when Napoleon Bonaparte was exiled to St. Helena, an island located some 800 miles away, that the United Kingdom finally established a military outpost Ascension to keep tabs on him (a good idea since he’d escaped exile once before).

Some of the most colorful descriptions of Ascension come from naturalists arriving at the island in the decades following British settlement. Among these voices was a young Charles Darwin, who arrived on the island in the summer of 1836 and described it as possessing a “naked hideousness.”

“Those who have beheld a volcanic island, situated within an arid climate, will be able at once to picture to themselves the aspect of Ascension,” Darwin wrote. “To complete this desolate scene, the black rocks on the coast are lashed by a wild and turbulent sea.”

However, a little less than two centuries after this bleak description, the island is now a lush tropical cloud forest filled with eucalyptus, bamboo, banana plants, araucaria, and Cape bramble—all plants from three separate continents. So how did this happen? Well, the short answer is humans, but the slightly longer answer is the work of the British botanist Joseph Hooker. In 1847, Hooker persuaded the Royal Navy to bring plant specimens from the Kew Gardens in London to catch rain, reduce evaporation, and improve soil health, according to El Pais.

The introduction of these plants, along with more humans (who brought with them insects, rats, and cats, in a cyclical parade of invasive species), essentially terraformed the island, turning a once desolate landscape into something more suitable for human habitation.

Some scientists see this history as a possible blueprint for fighting desertification, which is spreading as climate change threatens vulnerable ecosystems. Among them is Victor Maull, who recently finished a Ph.D. at Pompeu Fabra University focused on the island.

“In the laboratory we are working to make minimal models that can explain changes to ecosystems,” Maull said in a press statement. “Normally, we model ecosystems that degrade, but with Ascension we have the opportunity to understand the reverse process and see if we can invert the collapse.”

However, other experts who spoke to El Pais have a different interpretation of Ascension island’s ecological history—one that stresses caution rather than celebration. Although Darwin had little positive to say about the island on his visit, endemic species did live on the roughly 34-square-mile island back then. Today, those native species are being crowded out by invasive plants that now cover almost the entire island. One of those natives, the Ascension Island parsley fern, was thought to be extinct until 2009, when researchers found four plants clinging to a cliff.

“What remains today is an unusual combination of species—bamboo, eucalyptus, ficus and others—that would never have grown or evolved together naturally in an ecosystem,” Tiffany Simpson, director of Conservation and Fisheries for the Ascension Island Government, told El Pais. Because of this mismatch, even some of the invasive plants are struggling to establish roots in the shallow, volcanic soil, causing many trees to topple over during fierce storms.

Whatever one makes of its history, Ascension offers two lessons. It shows that deliberate intervention may help hold back advancing deserts, and it warns of what can be lost when humans reshape a one-of-a-kind ecosystem to suit their own needs, whether on this planet or another.

#6464. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6463. Could Vitamin B12 Hold the Key to Treating a Rare Genetic Disorder?

A search for genes linked to lifespan uncovered an unexpected connection between RNA splicing, metabolism, and developmental disorders.

A mutation linked to a rare developmental disorder appears to interfere with more than the way cells process genetic instructions. Researchers discovered that it also disrupts vitamin B12-dependent metabolism in tiny roundworms. Supplying the vitamin restored key metabolic processes and corrected developmental abnormalities in the animals, raising questions about whether a similar approach could eventually help people.

The findings concern Verheij syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that causes developmental delays, growth problems, and short stature in children. The condition is associated with changes in a gene involved in RNA splicing, an essential process that prepares messenger RNA for protein production. During splicing, cells remove unnecessary sections of RNA and join the remaining pieces to form instructions that can be used to build proteins.

The discovery emerged from experiments with the roundworm C. elegans, a widely used model organism in biological research. Scientists were initially searching for genes that influence lifespan when they identified a mutation in a splicing-related gene associated with Verheij syndrome in humans. Worms carrying the mutation grew more slowly and remained unusually small, resembling some of the developmental problems seen in affected children.

Further genetic screening and metabolic analysis showed that the mutation altered biochemical pathways that depend on vitamin B12. These pathways support normal growth and cellular function. When researchers administered vitamin B12 to the affected worms, the disrupted metabolic processes returned to normal, and the animals’ developmental defects were corrected.

“We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism,” says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. “Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12.”

To investigate whether similar metabolic disruptions occur in humans, the researchers examined publicly available data from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at University Hospital Cologne, to obtain blood samples from patients with Verheij syndrome. The analyses provided evidence that metabolic pathways affected in the worms may also be altered in people with the condition.

However, the results do not establish that vitamin B12 supplementation can treat Verheij syndrome in humans. Additional research is needed to determine whether the metabolic changes contribute directly to patients’ symptoms and whether correcting them could provide clinical benefits. The findings also suggest that metabolic dysfunction may deserve greater attention in other genetic disorders involving defective RNA splicing.

“Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases,” says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. “A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term.”

Reference: “Vitamin B12 alleviates spliceosomopathy via phospholipid remodeling” by Jonathan Kölschbach, Hormos S. Dafsari, Emily Baum, Anna Löhrke, Chun Kew, Ivan Dikic, Wenming Huang and Adam Antebi, 7 August 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76295-9

#6462. Solving the Space Junk Crisis Isn't Just About Counting Trash—It’s About Control and Economics

If people ever think about cleaning up space debris, they typically think of something equivalent to a giant garbage truck in the sky, collecting lost astronaut tools and dead satellites then hauling them back down to Earth to be deposited in a landfill. But dealing with space debris doesnât work that way, and a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who we typically cover for his work on the Solar Gravitational Lens idea, makes a good argument as to why.

Dr. Turyshev has turned his attention to orbital debris at a critical juncture. According to the filings made to the FCC, SpaceX, the company that runs the largest satellite megaconstellation, had their Starlink satellites perform 144,404 collision avoidance maneuvers in the six months from December 2024 through May 2025. Even accounting for the fact that there are more Starlink satellites in orbit now than ever, that means, on average, each one is having to dodge a potential crash every week.

Fortunately, Starlinks themselves arenât exactly in the âdanger zoneâ of orbit. They typically orbit around 500-600 kilometers, along with other megaconstellations such as Amazonâs Kuiper and Chinaâs Qianfan. In the paper, Dr. Turyshev separates this orbit from those higher up. At 500-600, there is enough atmosphere left that the area is semi self-cleaning - dead satellites and debris in these orbits will burn up in a few years.

Fraser talks about the oribtal dance that keeps satellites from crashing into one another.

Higher up, though, there are bigger problems, both literally and figuratively. At around 850 kilometers, giant rocket stages from launches past lurk with no control, and little to no atmosphere to drag them down in a reasonable time frame. They could stay in orbit for decades or centuries and donât have any means of avoiding one another. When they inevitably collide, they will spray debris both into their own orbit but also into higher and lower ones, potentially causing even greater problems for the lower orbiting communications megaconstellations.

According to European Space Agency Data cited in the paper, about 96 percent of the long-term collision risk comes from these dead objects. And Dr. Turyshev further proves that, even if we stop launching rockets tomorrow, the amount of debris already up there would collide and shatter faster than nature can clear it.

This isnât a surprise to anyone who has been paying attention to the problem of space debris for any length of time. That orbital cascade, commonly known as Kessler Syndrome, has been a long-standing problem orbital dynamicists have been grappling with for decades. According to Dr. Turyshev, controlling it comes down to three separate levers.

Fraser talks about some techniques to remove space debris from orbit.

First, regulators have to ensure that satellites are designed to intentionally deorbit quickly once their missions end. Luckily, they are already moving in that direction, with the FCC recently introducing a rule requiring satellites to clear out within five years of retirement, rather than the twenty-five years that had held sway for the last few decades. According to the paper, if the reliability of disposal rises from 90 to 99 percent and a satelliteâs allowable afterlife is cut to five years, it decreases the environmental hazard by a factor of 50.

A second lever is better vision. Space Situational Awareness (SSA) systems are great at tracking large bulky objects, but terrible at smaller objects the size of a bullet. But even for larger ones, thereâs still a level of âfuzzinessâ that analysts have to deal with, which means they know a general box where an object is in space, but not its exact position. When that box is large, satellite operators waste precious fuel dodging objects that never really posed a threat in the first place.

Rather than trying to track every bolt and nut floating through space, Dr. Turyshev suggests that we need to concentrate on shrinking the uncertainty zone around potential high-risk close calls. That idea aligns directly with the real-world infrastructure upgrades that are happening through NOAAâs Traffic Coordination System for Space (TraCSS), which is expanding its pilot program to reach more commercial operators this year.

Fraser discusses whether there's a limit to how many satellites we can potentially launch.

The third lever is what to do with the semi-permanent debris thatâs already in space. Instead of launching expensive missions to deorbit and grab every single one of them, Dr. Turyshev suggests an alternative he calls Just-in-Time Collision avoidance. If two dead rocket upper stages are about to crash, operators could use ground-based lasers or small swarms of shepherd satellites to move a few meters out of the way just before impact. While not quite as much of a long-term solution (since it simply avoids the immediate problem), it does offer a much less expensive solution than attempting to deorbit everything.

Economic calculations will play a major role in any future space debris solution, and right now the market is broken, as Dr. Turyshev points out. Due to agreements in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, a private cleanup company cannot simply fly up to an abandoned Soviet rocket booster and deorbit it. Technically that rocket booster is still owned by the government that launched it (even if, in this case, that government doesnât technically exist anymore). Also, orbital space suffers from the âtragedy of the commonsâ, as one firm removing a rocket booster benefits all of the other companies with equipment in orbit, despite the cost not being spread amongst them.

Dr. Turyshevâs solution is to create contracts that would pay for verifiable reductions in long-term risk - in other words, it would incentivize companies like Astroscale, which are intending to remove space debris, to remove the most dangerous pieces first. This would be financed by governments, using money from âdisposal bondsâ that pay back if the satellite successfully orbits without active intervention from Astroscale or one of its competitors.

Ultimately, this seems like a reasonable framework to build a long-term plan for space debris mitigation. But there are still some issues - like sheer scale. Even at a 99% successful deorbit rate, with potentially millions of satellites in orbit that would still leave tens of thousands of derelict ones at any given time. And thereâs definitely no clear path forward to a successor to the Outer Space Treaty. But the longer we as a space-faring civilization ignore these issues the worse the problem is going to get. Hopefully this paper helps provide part of the impetus to push towards a formal adopted solution framework. Or at the very least start a more comprehensive conversation about it.

S.G. Turyshev - Orbital Debris in Earth Orbit: Operations, Stability, Control, and Market Formation

UT - What Will It Take To Reach Zero Space Debris?

UT - A New Net-Membrane Could Clean Up Some Tricky Space Debris

UT - Astronomers Use "Blind Stacking" to Uncover Invisible Space Junk Threatening Geosynchronous Orbit

This tiny inkwell contains an alphabetic inscription in ancient Etruscan, a language that has never been fully decoded.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell

This small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

The vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

According to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet shows that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#6460. Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in One of the Deadliest Cancers

Researchers have identified another potential approach to treating pancreatic cancer, with early experiments suggesting that blocking a protein could slow tumor growth and strengthen immune defenses.

Pancreatic tumors can be surrounded by tissue so dense that it compresses blood vessels, making it difficult for nutrients to reach cancer cells. Even under these conditions, the cells continue growing. How they obtain the materials needed to survive has remained an important question.

Researchers at Fox Chase Cancer Center have identified one way pancreatic cancer cells obtain cholesterol and other fats, known as lipids. Their study, published in Nature Cancer, also identified a protein that helps control this process and could offer a potential target for cancer treatment.

The research focused on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common type of pancreatic cancer. These tumors contain large numbers of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), cells that produce and organize connective tissue. As CAFs and their collagen fibers expand, they can compress nearby blood vessels, restricting the tumor’s blood supply.

Despite contributing to this nutrient shortage, CAFs also help cancer cells overcome it.

“We found that CAFs can act as a source of these nutrients,” said Edna Cukierman, PhD, a professor and co-leader of the Cancer Signaling and Microenvironment Program at Fox Chase and co-senior author of the study. “Using laboratory and animal models, we discovered that CAF units acquire cholesterol from the bloodstream and transfer it to nearby pancreatic cancer cells through a process called trogocytosis”

Trogocytosis occurs when one cell takes small pieces of another cell’s membrane during direct contact. In this case, pancreatic cancer cells acquire pieces of CAF membranes containing cholesterol and other lipids that support their survival and growth.

The researchers discovered that this transfer depends on a protein called anoctamin 6 (ANO6), which helps prepare the CAF membrane for the exchange.

“These findings help explain how pancreatic cancer cells obtain essential nutrients despite the unusual structure of the pancreatic tumor microenvironment,” said Igor Astsaturov, MD, PhD, a professor at Fox Chase and co-senior author of the study. “Cancer-associated fibroblasts are not passive bystanders. They actively support tumor growth by transferring lipids to cancer cells.”

When researchers reduced or eliminated ANO6 in CAFs, the cells became less effective at supporting pancreatic cancer cell survival. In mouse models, tumors supported by CAFs with functional ANO6 grew substantially faster than those without functional ANO6.

The same nutrient transfer process also appeared to interfere with the immune system.

Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) are immune cells that recognize and kill cancer cells. When these T cells come into contact with CAFs, they can acquire membrane material containing cholesterol. Excess cholesterol in the tumor environment can contribute to T-cell exhaustion, making these immune cells less effective at fighting cancer.

“With Serge Fuchs, professor at the University of Pennsylvania and co-author on the paper, we were surprised to find that the same cellular mechanism can benefit the tumor in two ways – by supplying cancer cells with lipids while also weakening cancer-fighting T cells,” said Astsaturov. “Targeting ANO6 could potentially disrupt both of these tumor-supporting functions at the same time.”

In mouse models, blocking ANO6 reduced cholesterol accumulation in T cells within tumors and improved markers of their activity. Laboratory experiments also showed that T cells exposed to CAFs with reduced ANO6 were better able to kill cancer cells.

The researchers then tested whether drugs that interfere with ANO6-dependent activity could slow tumor growth. In mouse models, treatment with niclosamide or clofazimine significantly reduced tumor weight. Niclosamide also reduced cholesterol delivery to pancreatic cancer cells.

These findings suggest that targeting ANO6 could both restrict a nutrient source for pancreatic tumors and improve the immune response against them. However, the results remain preclinical, and further research is needed to determine whether selectively blocking ANO6 would work as a treatment in patients.

Trogocytosis is also only one of several ways pancreatic cancer cells may obtain lipids. The researchers suggest that the drugs tested could potentially help treat other difficult cancers, although that possibility requires further investigation.

“We believe our findings identify ANO6 as a potential therapeutic target that could simultaneously disrupt the nutrient supply supporting pancreatic cancer cells and reduce the immune-suppressive effects of the tumor microenvironment,” said Astsaturov.

The findings also build on nearly a decade of research into how the tissue surrounding pancreatic tumors supports cancer growth.

“Excitingly, reducing ANO6 expression also disrupted the stromal synapse-mimicry circuit we previously identified, which coordinates tumor nutritional support, CAF-unit metabolism, and immune suppression. These findings position ANO6 as the missing mechanistic link that unifies nearly a decade of discoveries by our team,” said Cukierman.

Reference: “ANO6-mediated trogocytosis of cancer-associated fibroblasts promotes pancreatic cancer cell growth and immune suppression” by Charline Ogier, Akino Mercy Charles Solomon, Elena Bondarenko, Zhijing Wu, Zhen Lu, Quoc Thang Bui, Mayura R. Dhamdhere, Yingying Tang, Ludmila Recoules, Alena Klochkova, Linara Gabitova-Cornell, Battuya Bayarmagnai, Diana Restifo, Aizhan Surumbayeva, Débora B. Vendramini-Costa, Alexander Y. Deneka, Ralph Francescone, Anna C. Lilly, Alyssa Sipman, Jaye C. Gardiner, Tiffany Luong, Janusz Franco-Barraza, Aleksandr Dolskii, Mariia Dmitrieva, Kathy Q. Cai, Margret B. Einarson, Emmanuelle Nicolas, Andrei Efimov, Emily Megill, Nathaniel W. Snyder, Sven Miller, Mark Andrake, Natalie Phinney, Rolf Brekken, Jérôme Cros, Erica A. Golemis, Yunyun Zhou, Bojana Gligorijevic, Corinne Bousquet, Jonathan Soboloff, Serge Y. Fuchs, Edna Cukierman and Igor Astsaturov, 30 October 2026, Nature Cancer. DOI: 10.1038/s43018-026-01265-5
